title: How to watch the Carolina Panthers: Networks to know for reigning NFC South champs Can Bryce Young take another step forward this fall? Here's everything to know about Carolina's upcoming broadcasts. Steven Louis Goldstein 1
summary:
Former No. 1 draft pick Bryce Young won eight of his 16 starts last season. Jared C. Tilton / Getty Images
After the requisite hiatus, it’s time to Keep Pounding . We welcome back the Carolina Panthers as we wonder what that bear is doing .
Last year’s Panthers were truly all over the place. Their regular season included wins against the loaded Los Angeles Rams and the full-strength Green Bay Packers. They also lost to the lowly Arizona Cardinals and got swept by the New Orleans Saints. Carolina
full_text:
Former No. 1 draft pick Bryce Young won eight of his 16 starts last season. Jared C. Tilton / Getty Images
After the requisite hiatus, it’s time to Keep Pounding . We welcome back the Carolina Panthers as we wonder what that bear is doing .
Last year’s Panthers were truly all over the place. Their regular season included wins against the loaded Los Angeles Rams and the full-strength Green Bay Packers. They also lost to the lowly Arizona Cardinals and got swept by the New Orleans Saints. Carolina dropped its Week 18 finale versus the Tampa Bay Buccaneers … but still claimed its division at 8-9. Then came an all-time entertaining wild-card game , in which the Panthers took Matthew Stafford’s Rams to the brink.
Carolina showed a lot of heart in that 34-31 stinger and ultimately raised its own expectations for 2026. Bryce Young now has much-needed momentum for asserting himself as a franchise quarterback. Tetairoa McMillan returns out wide after winning Offensive Rookie of the Year. Fellow receiver Jalen Coker tries to build off of his playoff breakout.
This defense touts an elite cornerback pairing of Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, plus new linebacker upgrades with Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke.
Dave Canales’ crew is scheduled for three primetime games before schedule flexing, including one at home when they host the Detroit Lions for “Sunday Night Football” in Week 4.  Here’s your guide to local and national viewership. Follow the team on The Athletic. Our beat writer, Joseph Person , is the 2015 Cam Newton of Panthers reporters.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside former Panthers star tight end Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The Panthers play in the final Monday night game of November when they visit the Buccaneers in Week 12; it airs on ESPN only. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past, at least.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
The Panthers are set to appear on TNF once this season when they head to Green Bay in Week 8.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.

title: Panthers' new-look offensive line ready to 'come with that smoke' vs. Bears in Week 1 Joseph Person 5
summary:

CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Taylor Moton and Ikem Ekwonu worked with trainers during the Carolina Panthers’ Labor Day practice, as they have most days after the team reported to training camp seven weeks ago.
The two veteran offensive tackles later visited with teammates in the locker room at Bank of America Stadium,
full_text:
The Panthers offensive line — from left, Monroe Freeling, Rob Hunt, Luke Fortner, Damien Lewis and Rasheed Walker — takes on a different look to start the season. Melina Myers / Imagn Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Taylor Moton and Ikem Ekwonu worked with trainers during the Carolina Panthers’ Labor Day practice, as they have most days after the team reported to training camp seven weeks ago.
The two veteran offensive tackles later visited with teammates in the locker room at Bank of America Stadium, where they’ll attend Sunday’s season opener against the Chicago Bears, but both will be sidelined for the Bears game and at least the three after it as they make their way back to full health.
The Panthers have known they would be without their starting bookend tackles for the start of the season, but their absences felt a little more real last month after the Houston Texans edge rushers dominated the replacements for Moton and Ekwonu during a joint practice that tilted heavily in favor of the Texans defense.
The Texans sacked quarterback Bryce Young seven times and intercepted him twice during a practice Panthers coach Dave Canales described as “lopsided.” At least four of those sacks came against rookie right tackle Monroe Freeling, who was overmatched by the edge-rushing tandem of Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter, who combined for 27 sacks in 2025.
The Panthers are chalking up Freeling’s struggles as a rough day against the NFL’s top-ranked defense from last season rather than a cause for alarm for their first-round pick.
“Those two guys (Anderson and Hunter), you don’t see those — you may see them one time a year, and that’s there (at Houston). And now you may see them with the Rams with those guys, right?” said right guard Rob Hunt, referring to Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald.
“But you don’t see that every week. (Freeling) has been holding his own. He’s been doing a really good job. And he’s a rookie, man. I remember when I was a rookie trying to block people; it’s hard. And not guys like that. I couldn’t imagine blocking some guys like that.”
After Ekwonu ruptured his patellar tendon in the playoff loss to the Los Angeles Rams, the Panthers signed veteran tackle Rasheed Walker to a one-year deal in free agency, then drafted Freeling with the 19th pick a month later. Many draft analysts viewed Freeling as a developmental pick after he started just 17 games at Georgia, but that learning curve was expedited after the Panthers found out this summer Moton was diagnosed with a blood clot in his lung .
So the Panthers will roll out an offensive line against Chicago featuring three new starters. In addition to the tackles, center Luke Fortner will make his Panthers debut after agreeing to a one-year contract to succeed Cade Mays, who left in free agency. Hunt is back after missing the final 15 regular-season games last year following biceps surgery before returning for the wild-card game.
“Don’t get me wrong, T-Mo and Ickey are huge parts of this O-line, and they have been for years. And everybody’s seen when this line is completely healthy what it can be and what it is. So we can’t replace them, right?” Hunt said Monday.
“But we can get guys that are really good football players like Monroe Freeling and Rasheed Walker, and they come in and do what they do. And also we’ve got Luke, who’s new. And I haven’t played in a year. So s—, we’re excited to go out for the challenge.”
The Panthers did a decent job protecting Young last season despite missing Hunt. Their 35 sacks allowed tied for the 12th fewest in the league.
Walker was known more for his pass protection than run blocking while starting 48 games the last three seasons for the Green Bay Packers. The 2022 seventh-round pick from Penn State allowed five sacks and 34 pressures last year, with a Pro Football Focus pass-blocking grade of 70.0 that ranked 42nd among 89 qualified tackles.
Walker faced the Bears three times last season with Green Bay, including a 31-27 playoff loss in which Chicago erased an 18-point halftime deficit at Soldier Field. Chicago might not have Houston’s pass-rushing firepower, but Montez Sweat finished with 10 sacks in 2025, the second-highest total of his seven-year career.
“He’s a strong pass rusher,” Walker said of the 30-year-old Sweat. “He’s a seasoned veteran, a respected pass rusher throughout the league.”
Sweat lines up on both sides of the line, so Walker and Freeling will see him Sunday, but the Bears are looking for someone else to step up on the edge. Austin Booker, who had 4.5 sacks last year, missed time late in training camp with a groin injury.
Canales spoke with Freeling during and after the Texans practice and doesn’t think he’ll carry it with him into the season.
“The good part about Monroe — really confident guy. He really enjoys playing ball,” Canales said. “I don’t wanna say happy-go-lucky because that wouldn’t be accurate in describing him, but he does have a self-deprecating nature to him, where he’s like, man, he’s acknowledging (how tough that day was).
“And I just told him, ‘Hey, if that’s not the best tandem, I don’t know what it is.’ This is what we need to take our steps and continue to improve stuff, but he’s excited about this week, and he’s had a couple of nice days of practice.”
The Panthers still believe the 6-7, 323-pound Freeling will be a franchise stabilizer at tackle. Left guard Damien Lewis said Freeling was the first offensive lineman on the practice fields during camp.
“That guy’s a freak. He’s real athletic, and he comes to work every day,” Lewis said. “He wants to learn. He’s hungry, and he’s just excited to be out here, just like every other rookie.”
Still, the team expects bumps in the road for Freeling as he makes the jump from college — even after playing in the SEC — to the pros.
“It’s a part of it,” Hunt said. “Anybody expecting a rookie to get in there and be flawless is either you’ve got really high standards for him, and you think he’s gonna be a Hall of Famer, because there’s only so many that does that, or you’re just delusional to the game of football.”
Walker called Freeling a coachable player with great length who benefited from blocking Jaelan Phillips every day this summer. As for Walker, the former Packer is fired up to see what this new-look offensive line can do against an opponent he knows well.
“It’s crazy. I think this is like my third time in a row playing the Bears,” said Walker, who saw Chicago in weeks 14 and 16 last year before the wild-card game. “Shoot, it’s the NFL. It’s a faceless opponent, honestly. We’re gonna prepare this week, game plan, and then we’re gonna come with that smoke on Sunday.”

title: Have Ben Johnson, Caleb Williams found the key to a new level of explosion for the Bears? Johnson is determined to maximize his quarterback's rare talent to operate outside the pocket, and Bears players have bought in. Dan Wiederer 16
summary:

Hang around Chicago Bears coach Ben Johnson long enough and it becomes easy to detect that look in his eye: the spark, the confidence of a solution-seeking leader who has identified an opportunity.
Bears coaches felt one of those familiar Johnson eagerness spikes last winter. Players recognized it in the early spring after Johnson pinpointe
full_text:
Caleb Williams' scrambling produced some magical moments in 2025, but the Bears believe they left a lot on the table as well. Patrick McDermott/ Getty Images
Hang around Chicago Bears coach Ben Johnson long enough and it becomes easy to detect that look in his eye: the spark, the confidence of a solution-seeking leader who has identified an opportunity.
Bears coaches felt one of those familiar Johnson eagerness spikes last winter. Players recognized it in the early spring after Johnson pinpointed a specific improvement target he believes can significantly boost the offense.
“There’s something here,” he told them. “There’s definitely something here.”
Johnson had done a comprehensive study of the Bears’ scramble drill video from last season and discovered messiness, promise and untapped potential. Even with an offense that vaulted from last in the NFL in total yardage in 2024 to sixth in Johnson’s first season — and from 28th to ninth in scoring — the coach’s thorough evaluation was filled with irritation, disappointment and eventually positivity, specifically with the Bears’ production on extended plays.
On so many occasions, thanks to the athleticism and artistry of quarterback Caleb Williams, the offense found ways to improvise when their original concept didn’t quite click. Any YouTube search of 2025 Williams highlights will return a compilation of such moments, almost always including the fourth-and-8 “Jumpman” magic trick that produced a 27-yard completion to Rome Odunze during the Bears’ playoff rally past Green Bay. ( Madden cover, anyone ?)
But too frequently and for myriad reasons, many similar plays became empty adrenaline rushes, near-misses, “Wow!” incompletions. Johnson estimates that, when Williams broke the pocket and threw downfield last season, the Bears connected at only about a 40 percent rate. Not good enough.
“He’s too good of a thrower on the run,” Johnson says. “Our guys are too good at separating for that not to be at a higher clip for us. There are big plays there to be had. … I think that’s something Caleb can really sink into. I think we can make a huge jump.”
Receivers coach and assistant coach Antwaan Randle El agrees, calling last year’s extended play inventory both “frustrating” and “encouraging,” and believing the Bears should have done much more damage. Sometimes Williams wasn’t precise enough with his passes or was a tad too helter-skelter on the move. In other instances, receivers weren’t urgent enough in the way they came alive for the ensuing scramble. Or they simply didn’t create enough separation or secure a catchable pass.
“It’s like, ‘Dude, we made these (plays); why didn’t we make that one?’” Randle El says. “It just comes down to small things we have to adjust.”
That is precisely why Johnson’s enthusiasm has elevated with confidence that an entire unit — quarterback, pass catchers, blockers — will collaborate on a season-long endeavor that’s part science experiment, part art project, part traffic study. There’s something here indeed. But collective ownership is required.
In a best-case scenario, the Bears’ troubleshooting efforts might soon become a production cheat code, perhaps as early as Sunday when they open the season at Carolina.
Says Williams: “This is a piece of our offense that will help make us one of the most explosive, if not the most explosive offense in the league.”
As sacrilegious as this might sound to devout Bears fans, Johnson was equipped inside Halas Hall this offseason with Green Bay Packers highlights as a teach tape. That’s nothing new around the league with peak Aaron Rodgers, a four-time league MVP, propped up as a maestro with elite ability to orchestrate an entire offense through an extended play.
The Packers’ archived videos speak for themselves.
“They were very defined with what they were doing,” Johnson says. “You could tell they coached it. You could tell Aaron really believed this was a big play waiting to happen — whether it’s a throw down the field or whether it’s a chance for (defensive pass interference). And all their guys reacted that way.”
Thus, that’s what Bears coaches highlighted. The response time. The urgency. The stamina.
The non-verbal communication. The understanding of where to go and how to get there.
“These are great opportunities for big plays,” Johnson says, “particularly with the style of quarterback Caleb is. We’ve got to use that.”
The green-and-gold tutorial wasn’t new for tight end Cole Kmet. For two seasons, he played under former Bears coordinator Luke Getsy, who had three years of his own experience working with Rodgers in Green Bay. By extension, Kmet had received plenty of tutelage on how the Packers found their groove.
“A lot of it,” he says, “is learning to play with that style of quarterback.”
Perhaps it’s fitting then that two of the better examples of the Bears making the most of a scramble drill last season came at Lambeau Field — in Week 14 against the Packers, in the stadium where Rodgers so often became a football alchemist.
The first, during a third-quarter Bears touchdown drive, came after a play-action concept fizzled. Williams, amid pressure from blitzing safety Evan Williams, sprinted right to create space. And Kmet, recognizing both the “second play” opening and the space available down the field, turned up the right sideline with linebacker Isaiah McDuffie in his wake.
The resulting 26-yard completion — great vision, great timing, great touch on the throw, great body control on the catch — was among the prettiest sequences of the season.
. @CALEBcsw escapes and delivers a dime to @ColeKmet 🤩
📺: FOX | #ProBowlVote pic.twitter.com/WtTUmiRUbr
— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) December 7, 2025
“Cole made it known he was going vertical,” Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor says. “Caleb dropped it in on the sideline. Every time we show our teach tape, the guys are used to seeing those now.”
Three drives later, a 24-yard completion to receiver Devin Duvernay came with Williams exiting a noisy pocket, rolling right and waiting for his receiver — who originally had a deep route up the numbers to the left — to reset and sprint all the way to the right sideline.
Fastball. On target. First down.
“That becomes an explosive completion,” Taylor says, “simply because (Duvernay) just kept flying into the picture.”
Indeed, such extra effort is a big part of the equation. And for many Bears pass catchers who have never played with a quarterback quite like Williams, conditioning themselves — both mentally and physically — has become part of the process.
“Because Caleb has this ability,” Randle El says, “it has to become a part of who we are. And when he’s out of the pocket, our guys have to light up and be ready to go for him.”
New Bear Kalif Raymond, an 11th-year veteran, has made most of his career receptions from Ryan Tannehill, Marcus Mariota and Jared Goff. Raymond joked this summer that, with Williams and these Bears, “there’s no such thing as a love-of-the-game route.”
“The ball can always come your way — in any phase of the play.”
In some instances, that might be 10 or more seconds after the snap, with players in pattern needing to finish their original routes, then relocate their quarterback, then scan the field and get in sync.
“Another big part of it,” Kmet says, “is understanding the full concept that was called, too. You might know your route. But if you know where everyone else is or where they should be, OK, that can now kind of help with how do I properly get in phase with the quarterback? Where’s the open space going to be? If there’s somebody over top of me, I’ll probably not be able to take it there. So I’ll become more flat. It just puts a little more on the receivers and tight ends to understand the full picture of the concepts.”

full_text:
With Myles Garrett (and Aaron Donald) on board, the Rams are comfortable Super Bowl favorites. Katelyn Mulcahy / Getty Images
Not sure why we’re playing the season. The Los Angeles Rams have already been crowned champs, thanks to the addition of Myles Garrett and the return of Aaron Donald.
Never mind that their quarterback’s back could go at any second. Or that a team in their division actually won the Super Bowl last year and has a lot of great, young players. Yeah, the Seattle Seahawks get no respect.
But if the Rams don’t march through the league … and the Seahawks don’t repeat … then it actually does seem wide open. The Buffalo Bills, New England Patriots, Denver Broncos (I have Jaylen Waddle on every fantasy team), Philadelphia Eagles, Baltimore Ravens and even the Kansas City Chiefs and San Francisco 49ers could make a case. I am afraid, though, that the Houston Texans’ defense will be muttering about the offense again all season.
A lot of teams at the bottom might be tanking for Arch Manning, and there is no real new blood at quarterback this season. It’s the first time since 2022 that there won’t be a rookie quarterback starting in Week 1. (Fernando Mendoza is the 14th quarterback to go No. 1 since 2007, and all but Baker Mayfield and Jared Goff started the opener that season.)
Then again, when you have Kirk Cousins …
Last season’s record : 142-137-8 against the spread, 48-47 on best bets
All odds are from DraftKings and are locked when the pick was made. All times are ET.
The rematch that we assume the Patriots have been waiting for. And this time, they won’t have Kenneth Walker III to worry about. We should be tempted by the Patriots adding A.J. Brown and having a healthier offensive line this time … but we’re not. (Did you know the departed Stefon Diggs had better numbers than Brown — across the board, but especially in EPA/target: 0.68 to 0.25 — last year?)
Seattle has a much better defense than New England, and we also think Sam Darnold can improve in his second season with the Seahawks, new play caller and all.
Much of the talk about this game has centered on the teams’ opposite travel plans, with the 49ers arriving in Australia six days before the Rams. But this game might come down to the Rams having Garrett and new cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson.
The 49ers have a major hole at left guard, and on the other side of the trenches, their pass rush seems suspect. New defensive coordinator Raheem Morris loves to play zone, but that is playing right into Matthew Stafford’s hands if there is no pressure. Stafford ranked among the top four QBs in yards per attempt, explosive pass rate and EPA per dropback against zone from a clean pocket last season.
This is the safest Survivor Pool pick of the week other than the Jaguars. The Falcons have already taken a lot of hits on defense, and their quarterback stinks. Meanwhile, this is the freshest old man Aaron Rodgers will be all season, and the home crowd will be a factor in native son Mike McCarthy’s debut.
The Robert Saleh Bowl. The two teams to employ him as head coach square off, with the first team to score 20 points the likely winner. If you’re positive Cam Ward is a lot better than Geno Smith, this is an easy pick. I am not. Give me Breece Hall with a big game.
Remember how badly the Texans terrorized Josh Allen last season? What about in 2024, when he went 9 of 30 in Houston? I am sure he remembers.
It will be interesting to see how much of an impact new receiver DJ Moore has. I am skeptical because he had a habit of disappearing at his first two stops, but he does resemble Pac-Man at times. Moore ranks fourth in the NFL in yards after the catch (3,205) since being drafted in 2018, and the Bills had the seventh-most YAC last season (2,052). The Texans allowed the sixth-fewest YAC (1,587).
The Saints are getting a lot of love this season (including from me), but there are levels to this. The Lions have some question marks on defense, but they have a lot of talent and take care of business at home, with Jameson Williams taking another leap as a playmaker.
Did I mention the Ravens are my Super Bowl pick? No? Probably because I am not that crazy about it. But … the three NFC West teams will beat each other up, and I am not buying the Bills or Chiefs this season. Heck, might as well throw in another MVP for Lamar Jackson. The Ravens will lead the league in yards per carry (5.3 in 2025) again, and their improved pass rush will make life easier as well.
Obviously, the Browns are starting Deshaun Watson only because the first two games are on the road. If by some miracle he shows any resemblance to his 2020 (!) form, then they can figure out what to do with all the booing home fans. The thing is, the Browns do have a lot of young talent on the roster. It just won’t matter for a couple of weeks. Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars roll (they were 8-0 as favorites last season, winning by an average margin of 14.6 points).
My mom says most of the mean comments from my season total predictions came from Bengals fans, just because I am not sold on this new, improved defense (or the head coach). Well … another reason I like the under on 10.5 wins is that they always start the season slow. Since 2020, Joe Burrow has been sacked a league-worst 10 percent of the time in openers and has lost four times, a league-high.
The Buccaneers started 6-2 last season and 3-1 in 2024 and 2023. Give me Todd Bowles with a freshly paid Baker Mayfield fired up to show he doesn’t need Mike Evans.
We’re all for Week 1 shenanigans, and we’re calling for some immediate regression here, as the Bears won six games last season where they trailed with two minutes or less remaining. The Panthers added pass rusher Jaelan Phillips and linebacker Devin Lloyd, and the Bears are a little gimpy at receiver coming out of the gate. Home dog, please.
This one makes no sense to me. Only 5.5 points? The Commanders have no one to block for Jayden Daniels, and their defense isn’t good, either. Meanwhile, Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is skipping around because they finally got rid of Brown and have a competent play caller. Philadelphia wins its sixth straight season opener.
Go ahead: Name a Dolphins receiver. That’s what happens when you have $182 million in dead cap space. The Kirk Cousins Era starts with an easy win.
If you recall, I am big on the Cardinals over 3.5 wins this season. This is not one of them. The Chargers make a statement in this one, with new play caller Mike McDaniel letting Justin Herbert throw deep and getting Omarion Hampton 25 touches. A big reason is the return of offensive tackles Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt. The Chargers allowed a 33 percent pressure rate with them in 2024. That jumped to 43 percent without them over the past two seasons.
This spread has been the biggest mover of the week, as the Packers opened as favorites, but people have no faith in MarShawn Lloyd. (The Packers might not have much, either.)
However, Jordan Love’s explosive pass rate (21 percent) when Jayden Reed and Christian Watson were both on the field last season would have led the NFL. And it’s a revenge game for fired Cardinals coach Jonathan Gannon, the Packers’ new defensive coordinator, as he gets to go against one of his former quarterbacks, Kyler Murray.
The Cowboys overhauled their defense after giving up a league-worst 6.1 yards per play last season. And their offense is loaded, especially with George Pickens in another contract year. I plan to back the Giants’ defense — and professional coaching staff — often this season, but not in Week 1.
This one is another head-scratcher. Patrick Mahomes is coming off left knee surgery, his left tackle is injured and the Broncos led the NFL with 68 sacks last season, the fifth-most ever. Denver also has a very good run defense, which will delay Walker’s coming-out party as a fantasy football star by a week.
Best bets: Steelers, Ravens, Panthers, Jaguars and Broncos
Upset special…

There are no distractions, there’s a rejuvenated pass rush,
full_text:
Dexter Lawrence is the main piece of the Bengals' offseason defensive overhaul. Katie Stratman / Imagn Images
The optimism around Cincinnati about the Bengals in 2026 has crossed the threshold from cautious to concerning.
Feeling this good about the local football club days before the opener doesn’t sit well around these parts. Years of heartbreak and scar tissue produced real intuition.
This feels too good to be true for Bengals fans.
There are no distractions, there’s a rejuvenated pass rush, a division in transition, an easy schedule, five starters returning up front, mean Joe Burrow making comparisons to 2019 LSU, near-perfect health and, oh yeah, Dexter Lawrence.
The foundation and structure of the 2026 Bengals are the strongest they’ve been since 2022, coming off the Super Bowl. Even the two historically fatal problems for the Bengals now have quality solutions.
Joe Flacco is back (collecting a cool $6 million) in case the Burrow injury strikes again. The front office threw every asset imaginable at a defensive line capable of coming in waves and covering warts.
The urgency in the building and the locker room has been palpable, in large part because Burrow refuses to let off the gas. His aggressive leadership style and prognostications are not social catnip. They are genuine, impactful and drove what veteran Bengals dubbed the toughest camp in the Zac Taylor era.
There’s real cohesiveness and a sense of purpose that’s developed since the Lawrence trade sent shockwaves throughout the NFL and the home locker room at Paycor Stadium.
It’s fair to have flashbacks to the unraveling of the past three seasons. Those memories haven’t faded, and the broken trust should leave a healthy hesitancy about what comes next.
Forgetting the past and merely assessing the present, the Bengals are contenders and should be viewed as such.
On paper, a defense with an invigorated Lawrence at the center, one-on-one winners along the edges, a true shutdown corner in D.J. Turner and veterans on the back end projects to a solid group, not one responsible for another lost fall.
This feels different in 2026. This feels real. This feels like there’s reason to believe the recent past doesn’t apply anymore.
The plea since losing the AFC Championship Game to end the 2022 season was to keep putting Burrow in January and see what happens.
After three years away, Burrow should be back in the playoffs again. What happens next is what the football world — especially frighteningly optimistic Bengals fans — has been awaiting.
In my crystal ball, Cincinnati goes 12-5, wins the AFC North and makes a playoff run. There’s just too much going right internally to think it will fail.
Bengals 12-5 Ravens 11-6 Steelers 8-9 Browns 5-12
1. Texans 2. Bengals 3. Chargers 4. Bills 5. Ravens 6. Jaguars 7. Broncos
Bengals over Broncos Chargers over Jaguars Ravens over Bills
Texans over Ravens Bengals over Chargers
1. Rams 2. Lions 3. Cowboys 4. Buccaneers 5. Seahawks 6. Eagles 7. Saints
Lions over Saints Eagles over Cowboys Seahawks over Buccaneers
Rams over Eagles Lions over Seahawks
Defense: Cincinnati will set Taylor-era records for pressures and players with 40-plus pressures.
Last year, the Seahawks produced 392 pressures and 47 sacks in the regular season. The number of pressures and sacks only tells half the story. Seattle had six players create at least 40 pressures.
The Seahawks were the model when Cincinnati reimagined its defensive line this year. So much so that the Bengals snagged Seattle edge Boye Mafe for $20 million per year.
The Bengals built waves and defensive coordinator Al Golden sounds determined to deploy all of them.
A Bengals defense under Taylor has never managed more than three players with 40-plus pressures in a season, and there were only two last year (Joseph Ossai 43, Myles Murphy 41).
Here’s the history of pressures and players with 40+:
If all goes to plan, the Bengals could not only post a season best for pressures, topping 314 in 2023, but also double the number of 40-pressure players for a new mark.
Here’s a ranking of those most likely to cross the 40-pressure threshold:
Mafe: Crossed the 40 barrier each of the last three seasons for Seattle. Murphy: Notched 41 last year, including 28 in the final eight games. Lawrence: Averaged 53 pressures per season from 2021 to 2023. Topping out at 65 in 2023. Cashius Howell: Expectations are high, and he’ll be given many pass-rush opportunities. Jonathan Allen: From 2020-23, crossed the 40-threshold every season. B.J. Hill: Posted between 29-42 pressures and three to five sacks each of the last four seasons
How many opportunities each player ends up with because of injury or earned playing time increases will determine the top, but the many options illustrate the idea that this pass rush plans to use many different angles and skill sets.
Offense: The Bengals will have twice as many under-center runs and under-center play-action passes as last season.
How much will Cincinnati lean into the under-center offense this year? Will they stick with it, or will it become a lost footnote of the offseason program ? That will be an interesting question to watch unfold this year, but Burrow will see the fewest sacks and pressures per game of his career.
The depth, specifically at offensive tackle, leaves reason for pause, but there’s plenty to like about the offensive line. All five starters return, Dylan Fairchild and Amarius Mims appear to be developing into upper-crust players, and the line is coming off a second half of last season in which Burrow was kept extremely clean coming back off his toe injury.
In fact, 2025 produced the fewest sacks and pressures per game of his career.
With a dedication to the under-center game helping alleviate a percentage of high-difficulty protection situations and a chance to play from ahead more often, this sets up a chance for Burrow to further build on last year’s record and take those numbers below two sacks and the 10.8 pressures per game.
Special teams: Evan McPherson will go perfect from inside 55.
Perhaps nobody enjoyed a better camp than McPherson. He only missed once or twice all camp, depending on who you talk to. He connected on attempts from 61 and twice from 59 in the preseason. This follows a year when he didn’t miss a field goal inside 50.
He’s back with the exact same operation of long snapper William Wagner and holder Ryan Rehkow for a second straight season. This is the first time in his career he’s had the same holder-snapper as the previous year. His confidence shows.
Weather and circumstance can prove problematic, but the combination of confidence, power and continuity makes him a candidate to enjoy a career year in what’s already been a fantastic career for McPherson.
Overall: The Bengals will have at least one four-game winning streak.
Twice under Taylor, the Bengals ripped off a win streak of at least four games. The first came in 2022 when Cincinnati won 10 in a row before losing to the Kansas City Chiefs in the AFC Championship Game. The second came during the desperate final push in 2024, when Burrow led five straight wins to finish narrowly outside the playoffs. Perhaps these streaks are even-year trends, but considering how the schedule sets from Halloween to Christmas, it feels ripe for a hot streak where the Bengals catch momentum and stack victories.
Surviving the early part of the season will be critical for this team to take flight at the midpoint.

full_text:
Cleveland Browns cornerback Denzel Ward threw out the ceremonial first pitch before a Guardians game in 2024. David Richard / Imagn Images
CLEVELAND — Browns cornerback and Northeast Ohio native Denzel Ward is buying into his hometown MLB team, joining fellow NFL star Travis Kelce as a Guardians minority investor, the Guardians have announced.
The Guardians announced Kelce’s addition to the organization in May and, on Wednesday, the day of the NFL season opener, Ward has followed suit, purchasing a stake in the same minority group.
Ward, 29, grew up in the Cleveland suburb of Macedonia and attended Nordonia High School and Ohio State University. The two-year, $62 million extension Ward received from the Browns in late July should ensure the five-time Pro Bowler plays his entire career with the team that drafted him at No. 4 overall in 2018. Ward has 18 interceptions over 100 career games with the Browns and led the NFL with 19 pass breakups in 2024.
The Guardians’ ownership group is undergoing widespread change. The Dolan family, the longest-tenured owners in franchise history, purchased the team for $323 million in November 1999 after a failed bid to buy the expansion Browns. Four years ago, however, Paul Dolan struck an agreement with David Blitzer to become a minority owner with a pathway for Blitzer to eventually assume controlling interest.
Travis Kelce and Denzel Ward at the Cleveland Guardians game pic.twitter.com/FOZ2Mw0kI5
— BBQ Chiefs (@BBQChiefs) April 5, 2026
Blitzer’s first option to take over majority control is after the 2027 season, multiple industry sources told The Athletic under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Dolan has insisted he plans to stay on as a minority owner. He’ll have plenty of company, as Blitzer spearheaded the additions of Kelce and Ward. Both players sat in Blitzer’s suite for the Guardians’ home opener in April.
“Cleveland is my hometown,” Ward said in a statement. “I’m so blessed to be able to show up for this city on the field and now as a part of the Guardians organization.”
The Guardians plan to honor Ward at Progressive Field on Tuesday.
The Guardians had planned to celebrate Kelce’s involvement in June , but the day was rained out. The Kansas City Chiefs tight end instead signed autographs for fans from the players’ parking lot.
Blitzer co-owns the Philadelphia 76ers, who this summer landed their own star with Cleveland roots, as well as the New Jersey Devils, a forthcoming WNBA team and a NASCAR outfit with his business partner Josh Harris, through their venture, Harris Blitzer Sports Entertainment. Blitzer also has ownership stakes in a handful of soccer clubs throughout Europe.
In the spring, Forbes estimated the Guardians’ franchise value to be $1.66 billion, which ranked 26th out of the league’s 30 teams. The Guardians annually carry one of the league’s lowest payrolls.
John Sherman, a Kansas City businessman, originally came aboard as Dolan’s potential successor in 2016, but he divested his shares three years later to instead buy his hometown Royals. After Sherman shifted gears, he and Dolan shopped his stake for several years until they identified Blitzer as the right partner.
In a sit-down interview with The Athletic last summer, Sherman said he “would have made ties (in Cleveland),” but admitted, “It’s just different — to get to do this in your hometown is a pretty special deal, and it’s a rare opportunity.”
Albeit on a smaller scale, Kelce and Ward will get that opportunity.
— Zac Jackson contributed to this report.

title: The every-season Cowboys question: Is it realistic to think this could be the year? The NFC is loaded with the Seahawks, Rams, Eagles and more. It's an uphill climb for the Cowboys. Our experts dive into their pros and cons. Jon Machota, Jourdan Rodrigue and more 2

It’s been three decades since the Dallas Cowboys last played in a Super Bowl. While the franchise has had five or six teams capable of reaching the biggest stage, they haven’t even returned to the NFC Championship Game.
This year’s team has the makings
full_text:
It's been a long time since Jerry Jones, right, and the Dallas Cowboys have had postseason success. Can Dak Prescott help get them there this season? Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; Photos: Emilee Chinn, Ron Jenkins / Getty Images
It’s been three decades since the Dallas Cowboys last played in a Super Bowl. While the franchise has had five or six teams capable of reaching the biggest stage, they haven’t even returned to the NFC Championship Game.
This year’s team has the makings of being one of those groups capable of double-digit wins and a potential deep playoff run. That certainly wasn’t the feeling the previous two seasons at this time of year. But when something hasn’t happened for 30 years, understandably, most go with the “Yeah, I’ll believe it when I see it” approach.
Up until this week, everything had been heading in a positive direction for the Cowboys. The team announced after Monday’s practice that Tyler Smith, its best offensive lineman and arguably the top offensive guard in the game, will be out four to six weeks after needing left thumb surgery to repair damaged ligaments. Dallas should be able to keep things afloat until he returns, but it was especially notable because the Cowboys avoided any major injuries during training camp and the preseason.
Good health, no George Pickens contract drama, returning one of the league’s best offenses, and what appears to be a much-improved defense have created some noticeable positive vibes with this year’s team.
And this isn’t just a media or fan observation. Players have acknowledged as much.
“I mean it’s definitely different,” said Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott, who is entering his 11th season. “I’m optimistic going into every season kind of with that mindset. It’s an NFL season; positive vibes and good energy doesn’t win you games. So understanding that we’ve put ourselves in a great position, we put ourselves right where we need to be to go and give ourselves the best chance to have a great week of practice and win Week 1 up there in New York.
“Right now, the energy and everything is great, but we got to make sure we’re doing everything to be accountable to each other and just continue on that trajectory. We’ve got to go do it. We’ve got to go win games.”
Others in key positions around the NFL have also taken notice. The Athletic ’s Mike Sando recently polled six executives about the NFC , having each rank all 16 teams. The Cowboys finished fourth behind the Los Angeles Rams, Seattle Seahawks and Philadelphia Eagles. One executive ranked the Cowboys as high as second. None ranked the team lower than eighth. Three executives called them Super Bowl contenders.
“It’s easy to talk,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said Monday. “We put our (Super Bowl) goals out there for the world to see and hear and debate, and it’s OK. It’s the way we want to be, because we do believe in ourselves and we have a lot of confidence. … I think what Dak’s talking about with all the positive vibes is real.”
To get a little different perspective on how the Cowboys are viewed nationally entering this season, we asked The Athletic ’s Jourdan Rodrigue, Jonathan Jones and Zak Keefer five questions to get their take on this year’s team.
Rodrigue: This is a well-coached, well-built team with elite talent at multiple premium positions — most specifically: quarterback, receiver and defensive tackle (I would count Quinnen Williams as the rare example of an interior defensive lineman in the “premium position” category). The Cowboys’ offensive structure, especially, makes them incredibly difficult to defend. They are multiple threats in the pass and run game, so defenses have to essentially pick which type of offense they can stomach allowing points and yards, for the sake of stopping a more powerful attack (the “pick your poison” cliché). Their offensive line is good and can be great (with more variance possible now that starting guard Tyler Smith will be out 4-6 weeks). Their scheme is ahead of the curve.
Defensively, the vision to significantly raise the floor is clear despite remaining questions about personnel. One of the best qualities a Super Bowl contender has is that it knows what it is, and knows what it is not (and can adjust to mask that). I don’t yet know whether Dallas is a Super Bowl contender, but for once, it has this quality.
Jones: Their offense and, specifically, their quarterback. Someone once said to me Dak Prescott is the most talked-about player in the NFL, and I had no good counterargument. Put Prescott in a Los Angeles Chargers uniform, and he’s regularly in the top-five discussion. Each year, half the NFL cycles through offensive coordinators, and though there are contrary examples, continuity matters. Brian Schottenheimer has been working with Prescott since 2023. Couple that with a great offensive mind in Klayton Adams (shoutout Jourdan), and Dallas has an edge.
Keefer: While the offense has all the makings of a top-three unit, at least — Dak Prescott isn’t thinking top three, he’s thinking No. 1 — it’s the other side of the ball that offers real opportunity. Simply put, the Cowboys cannot be worse on defense than they were a year ago: dead last in EPA per play, dead last in third-down percentage, dead last in passing yards allowed. Jerry and Stephen Jones were so impressed with Christian Parker in the interview process that they broke out of their comfort zone and hired a first-time coordinator. For years, without exception, Dallas recycled former head coaches for that role.
With some much-needed additions, starting with first-round pick Caleb Downs, this unit should be far more respectable this season. Paired with an elite offense, that could translate into three or four more wins.
Rodrigue: This team has talked about wanting to be in the Super Bowl conversation. They’ve been neutral to poor over the last several seasons, and that brings complacency. Sometimes teams with continuity must talk themselves out of complacency however they can, even as competitive as they are. But they also have to stay realistic about where their personnel is still limited (the secondary) and be ready to take big swings if they see the opportunity ahead of the trade deadline. No second-guessing, no half-measures … no complacency. Let it rip.
Jones: Themselves. And I don’t mean to sound annoying, but I have found it curious how openly the Cowboys have talked about the Super Bowl. It obviously is the reason everyone plays the game, but their offseason talk stands out because they’re the only team of 32 talking like that. They have won two playoff games in a decade and are 18-14 in December and January the past five seasons. Do Dallas know what it takes to make such a playoff run?
Keefer: The secondary. This unit couldn’t stop a nosebleed last year. It should be better this fall, thanks to Parker’s scheme and some new faces, and the regular-season schedule isn’t exactly loaded with top-tier quarterbacks. This unit has plenty of opportunities to gel by November, when the schedule softens a bit before a potential playoff push. The issue with making a deep postseason run? There’s nowhere to hide. Putting together two or three clean games in the defensive backfield might be too tall a task for a unit that’s still on its way up. I’m proceeding with caution.
Jones: If the Cowboys are going to reach their goals, Parker has to be to Dallas what Steve Spagnuolo was to the 2007 New York Giants. It’s been done before, and it will be done again. The hype around Christian Parker is real. Philadelphia knew it would lose him and still hated to see him leave. The Cowboys immediately involved him in free agency and draft prep. As much as you can invest in a 34-year-old stranger from a division rival to turn around your defense, Dallas has.
Keefer: Yes, it can be done. Look at what Josh McDaniels did last year with the New England Patriots’ offense. Look at what Liam Coen did with the Jacksonville Jaguars’ unit.…

full_text:
Sam Darnold's Seahawks beat the Rams in two out of three meetings last season, including in the NFC Championship Game. Jane Gershovich / Getty Images
RENTON, Wash. — Rest assured, all is well with Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold’s Super Bowl ring.
During the Seahawks’ ring ceremony in June, Darnold dropped his , but it emerged from the short fall unscathed.
“Of course this would happen to me, dropping the ring,” Darnold said Monday. “But I will say in my defense. … I opened the box, and the ring was already falling out. It wasn’t like I made the ring fall out of the box. I just wanted to clear that up.”
Likewise, the Seahawks want to make it abundantly obvious that they have no intention of living in the past. Seattle begins its title defense on Wednesday with a Super Bowl rematch against the New England Patriots in both teams’ season opener at Lumen Field.
Thanks to a family member with plenty of expertise on the matter, veteran defensive lineman Leonard Williams knows a tough task awaits the Seahawks. They hope to become the ninth franchise in NFL history to win back-to-back Super Bowls.
Williams’ father-in-law is Hall of Fame safety Ronnie Lott, who secured consecutive Super Bowl titles (plus two others) with the San Francisco 49ers in 1989 and 1990.
“He talked about how hard it is to repeat,” Williams said. “That was part of what he told me that’s hard about it: Guys look to the last season instead of looking forward, and we’re not doing that around here.”
Nor are the Seahawks getting googly-eyed about all the hype surrounding the Los Angeles Rams, either. Los Angeles is the clear favorite to win the Super Bowl with +500 odds. This year features the largest preseason gap between the top two teams in Super Bowl odds since the 2017 Patriots (+275) opened as favorites over the Seahawks, Green Bay Packers and Las Vegas Raiders (all +800). Seattle is tied for fourth in preseason odds at +1200, behind the Rams, Buffalo Bills and Baltimore Ravens (both +1000).
The Rams, who finished runner-up to the Seahawks in the NFC last year, added reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett, cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson and coaxed three-time DPOY Aaron Donald out of retirement. Seahawks safety Julian Love admitted it would be naive to say he has not paid attention to the Rams’ latest additions.
“But at the same time, I feel like, ‘How can we let that affect anything we do right now?’ is kind of the mindset,” Love said of the Rams. “We play those guys in December at some point. It’s September. It’s that mindset of, ‘We have more things to worry about.’ The biggest fish to fry is the one that’s right in front of us, and that’s New England.”
To Love’s point, the Seahawks won’t see the Rams until Christmas Day in Seattle. The teams will meet again two weeks later for the regular-season finale in Los Angeles. In the meantime, the Seahawks have been busy getting adjusted to first-year offensive coordinator Brian Fleury’s system ahead of Wednesday’s season opener.
Backup quarterback Drew Lock said the praise for the high-flying Rams hasn’t come up a lot in Seattle’s locker room. That’s not because the team is seeking to avoid the topic; rather, there just isn’t much time for those kinds of discussions.
“If I was in Sam’s shoes, I wouldn’t be going home thinking about what people are necessarily saying,” Lock said of Darnold. “I’d be thinking about what my kid’s eating for dinner, and is he actually going to eat it, or is he going to throw it on the ground?”
It helps, too, that the Seahawks would like to avoid being satisfied. Linebacker Ernest Jones IV said complacency would be Seattle’s pitfall, should the team fall short of expectations in 2026, a sentiment Williams echoed.
“You can win it all and just think you’ve got it all figured out,” Jones said. “The other 31 teams are evolving, and they’re trying to get better. They’re trying to get to where you are.”
With the way the Rams retooled their roster, they might have a deeper squad on paper than Seattle. But the Seahawks return reigning Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba, all five starting offensive linemen and many key contributors from the “Dark Side,” Seattle’s vaunted defense that allowed the fewest points per game in the league last season.
Having a sparkling recent track record doesn’t hurt Seattle’s cause, either, especially when it comes to winning over players like Love. The first three years of the safety’s career were spent on New York Giants teams that posted sub-.500 records.
“Success accelerates trusting the process,” Love said. “I’ve been in some places where you lose some games or some things go left, and you’re like, ‘Man, this process isn’t working.’ And so, it’s very easy for us to trust the process because we had success last year. We just feel good about how we go about work each day. We know nobody’s short-cutting anything.”
Still, it will be a challenge for Seattle to defend its crown, and not simply because one of its division rivals is the favorite to win it all. Williams expects the Seahawks to receive their opponents’ best each week.
In the process, Williams hopes Seattle can forge a new identity. The Seahawks will have their first opportunity to do so Wednesday.
Then, in due time, they can shift their attention to the Rams — regardless of whether they’re duking it out for a spot in the Super Bowl.
“Coming off of a successful year, we’re not trying to chase the previous team that we once were,” Williams said. “Even though that was just a year ago or months ago, we understand that it’s a whole new season and whole new team.”

full_text:
The Athletic staff has high expectations for the Texans’ defense, Bills quarterback Josh Allen and Sean McVay's Los Angeles Rams. Will Tullos / The Athletic; Bryan M. Bennett, Alex Slitz, Soobum Im / Getty Images
The 2026 NFL schedule isn’t messing around: It starts with a Super Bowl rematch between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks on Wednesday night, and then turns to the remade Los Angeles Rams, who will debut their stacked roster Thursday in a NFC West showdown with the San Francisco 49ers in Australia. By the time Patrick Mahomes and Bo Nix return from serious injuries to face off in an AFC West rivalry game Monday night, the NFL conversation will be filled with snap judgments and rash predictions.
But why wait until then? The Athletic’s NFL writers and editors already submitted their season-long predictions and projections, weighing in on the most exciting rookies, the coaches with the hottest seats, the teams that are most likely to surprise or disappoint and whether anyone can stop those juggernaut Rams.
Below are our consensus picks for MVP, Super Bowl champion, Offensive and Defensive Player of the Year and more. Forty staff members responded (with some opting not to answer everything, so some questions don’t have 40 responses). More than half of our voters picked the Rams to win it all. But eight other teams received at least one nod, and bear in mind that last year’s picks favored the Baltimore Ravens, Buffalo Bills and Kansas City Chiefs — while not a single staffer pegged the eventual champion Seahawks. Here are The Athletic’s staff picks for the 2026 season.
Quarterbacks have claimed this honor 13 straight times, and our panelists all voted for that trend to continue. There was less agreement over whether there would be a repeat winner; 23 voters chose a previous MVP to claim the award, while 17 gave votes to other candidates, with Joe Burrow leading the way in that category.
While it’s easy to talk yourself into some of the other leading MVP contenders — Lamar Jackson with a new coaching staff in Baltimore, Justin Herbert with Mike McDaniel calling plays in Los Angeles, Burrow (presumably) with an actual defense in Cincinnati and last year’s runner-up, Drake Maye, with a new weapon in New England — it’s too hard, for me at least, not to write down Josh Allen’s name here. No player tilts the axis of a football game more consistently; at this point, his levels of production are being taken for granted. Eight seasons in, Allen has piled up 79 rushing touchdowns and 299 total touchdowns, both records by a quarterback. Those figures are simply ludicrous. He has a new target in veteran wideout D.J. Moore, whom he meshed well with in the preseason. My bet is Allen is on the verge of his second MVP season. — Zak Keefer, senior writer
When Joe Burrow plays a full season, he's an MVP candidate (or a Super Bowl QB). So this is a bet on him staying healthy and the Bengals winning the AFC North, which I think they do if Burrow is healthy. Austin Mock's QB Index has Burrow at No. 1 and so does Jon Greenberg's QB (goes to thesaurus.com ) Register. — Jon Greenberg, columnist
Lamar Jackson clearly wasn't healthy last year — even after his return from injury. The Ravens felt change in the coaching department was necessary, and I believe Jackson and new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle will make for an explosive match. A healthy Jackson can still keep plays alive that are long dead for most quarterbacks, and the new environment might be what Jackson needs to deliver another MVP-level season. — Zac Jackson, Browns beat writer
The Cowboys' offense is a fireworks show, and it should be even better statistically than last year, given it will have some actual support from a defense that can't possibly be so bad. If the defense approaches even average, the Cowboys might win 12 or 13 games, which would put Dak — who was the MVP runner-up when Dallas won 12 games in 2023 — on the short list. — David DeChant, senior editor
If MVP is about quarterbacks, this award has become synonymous with the best running back or wide receiver, one of which has claimed it seven straight years. All but one of our votes went to those positions, with Jahmyr Gibbs, the highest-paid running back in NFL history, earning the most support. The man whose contract Gibbs surpassed, Bijan Robinson, received the second-most votes among running backs, while last year's winner, Seahawks receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, received only three votes to repeat.
He's been paid, so the Lions have no reason not to give Jahmyr Gibbs the Christian McCaffrey treatment. I'll be bold and say Gibbs touches the ball 400-plus times, and when a back as electric as Gibbs touches the ball that often, awards usually follow. — Jim Ayello, senior editor
Texans star Will Anderson Jr. finished second to Myles Garrett for this award last year, and those two pass rushers monopolized the votes this summer. A slim majority of our voters gave the edge to Anderson, who, like Gibbs, recently reset the market at his position.
Will Anderson Jr. would have won the award in 2025 if not for Myles Garrett, and though Garrett could have more opportunities on a winning team with the Rams in 2026, I think it's more likely he sacrifices some production to the rest of L.A.'s terrifying front. Anderson also has competition on his own team (Danielle Hunter), but he's clearly the best player on what should be the NFL's best or second-best defense. — DeChant
Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price, former teammates at Notre Dame, were the first two running backs chosen in April's draft, the first time that's happened for college teammates since the merger. They were also the most popular picks for this honor, ahead of the Tennessee Titans' Carnell Tate, the first wide receiver drafted.
A pair of pass rushers, Rueben Bain Jr. of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and David Bailey of the New York Jets, led Dallas Cowboys safety Caleb Downs in the voting. All three players were taken in the top 15 of the draft. Bain "appears to have a chance to make scouts look foolish for doubting him," according to The Athletic 's Ted Nguyen, while Bailey "was dominant at times this summer for the Jets, most impressively in joint practices against a solid Tampa Bay Buccaneers offensive line," according to Jets beat writer Zack Rosenblatt.
"The best player in the world is coming off a serious knee injury and appears as healthy as possible for someone who is less than nine months removed from surgery," as one of our editors put it, which is the argument in favor of Mahomes, the runaway leader here. Many of our voters submitted their ballots before Aaron Donald announced his return; the three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year also has an obvious comeback storyline, after two seasons away from the sport. Another intriguing option: Jayden Daniels, the 2024 Offensive Rookie of the Year who was limited to seven games because of injuries last season.
Three of the four leading vote getters in last season's poll wound up losing their jobs before the playoffs began, so this list might not be a comfortable place for the guys in the corner offices. The clear leader this year, Jets coach Aaron Glenn, is only in his second season running the franchise. The second most common pick, Washington's Dan Quinn, is entering his third season. Todd Monken, who has yet to coach a game for the Browns, received a vote. Tough business.
More than a third of the league's teams received nods here, although only one team, the New Orleans Saints, got more than five votes. The nominees ranged from some of the worst teams in 2025 (the Tennessee Titans and New York Giants) to several playoff teams, including the Houston Texans and Carolina Panthers.
I think the Saints offense can be sneaky good. Tyler Shough is flying under the radar at quarterback and Chris Olave, Travis Etienne Jr., Juwan Johnson and rookie top-10 pick Jordyn Tyson (once he returns from a hamstring injury) make for an…

full_text:
With Myles Garrett (and Aaron Donald) on board, the Rams are comfortable Super Bowl favorites. Katelyn Mulcahy / Getty Images
Not sure why we’re playing the season. The Los Angeles Rams have already been crowned champs, thanks to the addition of Myles Garrett and the return of Aaron Donald.
Never mind that their quarterback’s back could go at any second. Or that a team in their division actually won the Super Bowl last year and has a lot of great, young players. Yeah, the Seattle Seahawks get no respect.
But if the Rams don’t march through the league … and the Seahawks don’t repeat … then it actually does seem wide open. The Buffalo Bills, New England Patriots, Denver Broncos (I have Jaylen Waddle on every fantasy team), Philadelphia Eagles, Baltimore Ravens and even the Kansas City Chiefs and San Francisco 49ers could make a case. I am afraid, though, that the Houston Texans’ defense will be muttering about the offense again all season.
A lot of teams at the bottom might be tanking for Arch Manning, and there is no real new blood at quarterback this season. It’s the first time since 2022 that there won’t be a rookie quarterback starting in Week 1. (Fernando Mendoza is the 14th quarterback to go No. 1 since 2007, and all but Baker Mayfield and Jared Goff started the opener that season.)
Then again, when you have Kirk Cousins …
Last season’s record : 142-137-8 against the spread, 48-47 on best bets
All odds are from DraftKings and are locked when the pick was made. All times are ET.
The rematch that we assume the Patriots have been waiting for. And this time, they won’t have Kenneth Walker III to worry about. We should be tempted by the Patriots adding A.J. Brown and having a healthier offensive line this time … but we’re not. (Did you know the departed Stefon Diggs had better numbers than Brown — across the board, but especially in EPA/target: 0.68 to 0.25 — last year?)
Seattle has a much better defense than New England, and we also think Sam Darnold can improve in his second season with the Seahawks, new play caller and all.
Much of the talk about this game has centered on the teams’ opposite travel plans, with the 49ers arriving in Australia six days before the Rams. But this game might come down to the Rams having Garrett and new cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson.
The 49ers have a major hole at left guard, and on the other side of the trenches, their pass rush seems suspect. New defensive coordinator Raheem Morris loves to play zone, but that is playing right into Matthew Stafford’s hands if there is no pressure. Stafford ranked among the top four QBs in yards per attempt, explosive pass rate and EPA per dropback against zone from a clean pocket last season.
This is the safest Survivor Pool pick of the week other than the Jaguars. The Falcons have already taken a lot of hits on defense, and their quarterback stinks. Meanwhile, this is the freshest old man Aaron Rodgers will be all season, and the home crowd will be a factor in native son Mike McCarthy’s debut.
The Robert Saleh Bowl. The two teams to employ him as head coach square off, with the first team to score 20 points the likely winner. If you’re positive Cam Ward is a lot better than Geno Smith, this is an easy pick. I am not. Give me Breece Hall with a big game.
Remember how badly the Texans terrorized Josh Allen last season? What about in 2024, when he went 9 of 30 in Houston? I am sure he remembers.
It will be interesting to see how much of an impact new receiver DJ Moore has. I am skeptical because he had a habit of disappearing at his first two stops, but he does resemble Pac-Man at times. Moore ranks fourth in the NFL in yards after the catch (3,205) since being drafted in 2018, and the Bills had the seventh-most YAC last season (2,052). The Texans allowed the sixth-fewest YAC (1,587).
The Saints are getting a lot of love this season (including from me), but there are levels to this. The Lions have some question marks on defense, but they have a lot of talent and take care of business at home, with Jameson Williams taking another leap as a playmaker.
Did I mention the Ravens are my Super Bowl pick? No? Probably because I am not that crazy about it. But … the three NFC West teams will beat each other up, and I am not buying the Bills or Chiefs this season. Heck, might as well throw in another MVP for Lamar Jackson. The Ravens will lead the league in yards per carry (5.3 in 2025) again, and their improved pass rush will make life easier as well.
Obviously, the Browns are starting Deshaun Watson only because the first two games are on the road. If by some miracle he shows any resemblance to his 2020 (!) form, then they can figure out what to do with all the booing home fans. The thing is, the Browns do have a lot of young talent on the roster. It just won’t matter for a couple of weeks. Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars roll (they were 8-0 as favorites last season, winning by an average margin of 14.6 points).
My mom says most of the mean comments from my season total predictions came from Bengals fans, just because I am not sold on this new, improved defense (or the head coach). Well … another reason I like the under on 10.5 wins is that they always start the season slow. Since 2020, Joe Burrow has been sacked a league-worst 10 percent of the time in openers and has lost four times, a league-high.
The Buccaneers started 6-2 last season and 3-1 in 2024 and 2023. Give me Todd Bowles with a freshly paid Baker Mayfield fired up to show he doesn’t need Mike Evans.
We’re all for Week 1 shenanigans, and we’re calling for some immediate regression here, as the Bears won six games last season where they trailed with two minutes or less remaining. The Panthers added pass rusher Jaelan Phillips and linebacker Devin Lloyd, and the Bears are a little gimpy at receiver coming out of the gate. Home dog, please.
This one makes no sense to me. Only 5.5 points? The Commanders have no one to block for Jayden Daniels, and their defense isn’t good, either. Meanwhile, Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is skipping around because they finally got rid of Brown and have a competent play caller. Philadelphia wins its sixth straight season opener.
Go ahead: Name a Dolphins receiver. That’s what happens when you have $182 million in dead cap space. The Kirk Cousins Era starts with an easy win.
If you recall, I am big on the Cardinals over 3.5 wins this season. This is not one of them. The Chargers make a statement in this one, with new play caller Mike McDaniel letting Justin Herbert throw deep and getting Omarion Hampton 25 touches. A big reason is the return of offensive tackles Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt. The Chargers allowed a 33 percent pressure rate with them in 2024. That jumped to 43 percent without them over the past two seasons.
This spread has been the biggest mover of the week, as the Packers opened as favorites, but people have no faith in MarShawn Lloyd. (The Packers might not have much, either.)
However, Jordan Love’s explosive pass rate (21 percent) when Jayden Reed and Christian Watson were both on the field last season would have led the NFL. And it’s a revenge game for fired Cardinals coach Jonathan Gannon, the Packers’ new defensive coordinator, as he gets to go against one of his former quarterbacks, Kyler Murray.
The Cowboys overhauled their defense after giving up a league-worst 6.1 yards per play last season. And their offense is loaded, especially with George Pickens in another contract year. I plan to back the Giants’ defense — and professional coaching staff — often this season, but not in Week 1.
This one is another head-scratcher. Patrick Mahomes is coming off left knee surgery, his left tackle is injured and the Broncos led the NFL with 68 sacks last season, the fifth-most ever. Denver also has a very good run defense, which will delay Walker’s coming-out party as a fantasy football star by a week.
Best bets: Steelers, Ravens, Panthers, Jaguars and Broncos
Upset special…

full_text:
Running back Rhamondre Stevenson split time with TreVeyon Henderson last season, but he looks set to get the lion's share of the carries Wednesday in Seattle. Brian Fluharty / Imagn Images via Reuters
The New England Patriots couldn’t run the ball against the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl, so that became the biggest focus of the offseason. The Pats didn’t have a difference-maker on the outside, so they traded for A.J. Brown.
Now, with an opener against the Seahawks on the horizon, a first test of just how far Mike Vrabel’s team has come awaits. But perhaps the roster moves weren’t quite so reactive.
“I do not think that the Super Bowl was the only factor in the decisions that we made,” Vrabel said.
The 2026 Patriots season begins with more optimism than any since the departure of Tom Brady. Perhaps it’s not Super Bowl or bust, but this team should be a legit contender, and failing to win a playoff game would be a disappointment.
So as the season begins, let’s look at where things stand. (All stats are courtesy of TruMedia unless otherwise noted.)
This part should be obvious.
Drake Maye was the MVP runner-up with a so-so supporting cast in Year 1 of a new offense. Now, the Pats have given him a true No. 1 receiver in Brown, a solid No. 2 option in Romeo Doubs and what should be a better offensive line. He’s also back with Josh McDaniels. This could be the best passing offense in the NFL.
The less-talked-about area for improvement is in the red zone. The Patriots ranked 24th last season in the percentage of their red zone trips that resulted in points and 17th in red zone trips that resulted in touchdowns.
The early results from training camp indicate the passing success should be much better in that area. Brown is 6 feet 1, 226 pounds, and Doubs is 6-2, 210 pounds. That size matters in the red zone.
The Patriots’ top offensive priority in the offseason was becoming a more consistent running team after ranking only 22nd in the league in rushing success rate last season. The changes there are notable: signing tight end Julian Hill (who’s now hurt), fullback Reggie Gilliam and left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker.
But I’m not convinced they’ve done enough to make a meaningful difference.
In joint practices, the running game was just OK. Rhamondre Stevenson and (the currently injured ) TreVeyon Henderson split carries, and the guess here is they’ll get a similar number of touches this season. But it didn’t seem like there were a ton of holes for them to exploit.
The hope is that the Patriots’ passing game is so good that teams drop back into two-high-safety looks. Last season, New England faced the second-highest rate of eight-man boxes, a sign that opposing defenses didn’t respect the team’s wide receivers. Perhaps that would free up space for the backs.
But better running has to start with better blocking. Last season, the Patriots ranked 18th in yards before contact per rush. I’m not convinced that’s going to dramatically change.
If the top players on the back end stay healthy, this secondary will be one of the best in the NFL. The depth falls off quickly, but Christian Gonzalez is one of the game’s best corners, Marcus Jones is one of the game’s best slot corners, and Carlton Davis is a strong No. 2.
Oh, and safety Craig Woodson was phenomenal as a rookie in the playoffs, and now he’s playing next to Kevin Byard, the NFL’s interception leader last season.
The run defense is a bit worrisome, but the big concern on defense has to be the edge rushers.
The hope was that Harold Landry would return to the dominant player he was the first six weeks of last season. Instead, he remains out after not practicing all summer because of a lingering injury.
The hope was for second-round pick Gabe Jacas to play a big role. Instead, he missed all of the spring practices and the start of training camp, and his play in the preseason games reflected that.
Now the Patriots enter the season with Dre’Mont Jones as a starter on one side, even though pass rushing isn’t his speciality (it’ll be a drop-off from K’Lavon Chaisson), and an undrafted second-year player, Elijah Ponder, on the other.
It could work out great. Maybe Ponder turns into a legit starter, Jacas develops quickly and Landry recovers well. But that seems unlikely.
All eyes have been on Brown — and for good reason. He’s going to get much of the focus from opposing defenses.
But Doubs quietly put together an impressive second half of training camp and was especially good in the red zone.
He’s only 26, so he’s entering what should be the prime of his career, and the guess here is that he easily eclipses his career high of 724 receiving yards last season.
It’s wildly impressive that Woodson’s three best games last season, per Pro Football Focus’ charting, were all in the playoffs. For a rookie to play that well down the stretch that late into his first NFL season speaks volumes.
This season, look for Woodson to thrive in his second year in this defense and with Byard by his side.
Woodson was everywhere in training camp, and his blazing speed (4.45-second 40) is obvious.
I waffled all offseason between 10 and 11 wins. The schedule is harder, yes, but the roster is also better. The offense should be great. If the Patriots can be even a slightly above-average running team, the passing offense should be able to handle the rest.
The pause with the Pats is twofold. The first is that they lack depth and can’t afford injuries at multiple spots. The second is that edge rusher might be the most important position in the NFL outside of quarterback, and it’s this team’s weakest position.
We’ll learn a lot about Vrabel’s bunch in the season’s first month with four straight games (including three on the road) against playoff teams from a year ago. A 2-2 start would be totally fine.
Though I think Maye will be incredible, I have enough concerns about the defense and how it’ll stop the run that I’m predicting the Pats to go 10-7.
