full_text:
Drake Maye's Pats are off to the Emerald City, seeking revenge for their Super Bowl loss. Mark J. Rebilas / Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
The NFL’s newest season begins where its last one left off — with the New England Patriots, Seattle Seahawks and National Broadcasting Company.
A Super Bowl LX rematch is here to officially kick off the 2026 NFL campaign. No, Bad Bunny won’t be performing in the middle of this one, but there’s so much to look forward to in the season opener. The Seahawks raise their championship banner before the euphoric 12s. The Patriots seek revenge after February’s frustrating loss. It’s “Sunday Night Football” on a friggin’ Wednesday .
We’re all reporting as eligible tonight. Here’s what we can expect to see and hear from game No. 1 of 272.
NBC is free over the air. It’s also available with Peacock’s premium plan.
This is the third Week 1 to feature a Super Bowl rematch. It last happened in 2016, when the Denver Broncos beat the Carolina Panthers. This is the second time that an NFL season opens on a Wednesday — the Dallas Cowboys and New York Giants did it in 2012.
NBC has aired the season opener for more than two consecutive decades. The 2026 edition puts Mike Tirico on play-by-play and Cris Collinsworth on analyst duties. Melissa Stark and Kaylee Hartung are the corresponding field reporters. They were all on the call for Super Bowl LX, too.
There’s a pregame program called “NFL Kickoff Special.” It starts at 7 p.m. ET and is hosted by Maria Taylor. New Englanders will certainly recognize Devin McCourty, a 13-year defensive back for the Pats and a three-time Super Bowl champ . Everyone will recognize Mike Tomlin as he goes from unblinking head coach to studio staple. The desk also has NFL insider Mike Florio and enthusiastic clapper Jason Garrett.
Mike Macdonald’s Hawks were a two-way torpedo throughout 2025. They finished with the No. 3 scoring offense, No. 1 scoring defense and top seed in their conference. Despite a few offseason departures and the NFL’s ephemerality, Seattle takes the field as a viable back-to-back champ.
Kenneth Walker III is no longer in the backfield after signing with the Kansas City Chiefs. New Zealand native George Holani and Notre Dame draftee Jadarian Price will carry the load while last year’s RB2, Zach Charbonnet, recovers from knee surgery. The offense also replaces coordinator Klint Kubiak, who is now head coach of the Las Vegas Raiders. His successor, Brian Fleury, was tight ends coach and run game coordinator for the rival San Francisco 49ers.
Sam Darnold is back as QB1 and lead bird watcher . Jaxon Smith-Njigba is the reigning Offensive Player of the Year, looking to defend his receiving title amid double coverage. His presence frees up room for the steady Cooper Kupp and turbo-booster Rashid Shaheed.
The “ Dark Side ” defense boasts a disciplined front line and a secondary that can stuff the run. DL Leonard Williams and CB Devon Witherspoon are both fresh off of well-earned contract extensions. Derick Hall and Byron Murphy II return to the loaded pass rush; second-team All-Pro Ernest Jones IV holds down the second level. Newly signed defensive back Terrion Arnold won’t play in Week 1 as he remains on the commissioner’s exempt list while facing kidnapping and armed robbery charges.
Wednesday night begins an extended curtain call for sack artist DeMarcus Lawrence as well. The 13-year pro says that he will retire at the end of the season.
Like their opponents, the Patriots put together a dominant 2025. They went 14-3, ranking second in points scored and fourth in points allowed.
Then came an intense offseason. Coach of the Year Mike Vrabel was caught up in a scandal with Dianna Russini, who at the time was The Athletic ’s NFL insider . In June, the front office made a trade for A.J. Brown , one of the league’s best and most emotive players . There was also a protracted contract dispute with lockdown corner Christian Gonzalez, who received a record extension days before the start of the season.
On the sideline, Vrabel and offensive play caller Josh McDaniels are still at their posts. Zak Kuhr officially shifts from inside linebackers coach to defensive coordinator, while former DC Terrell Williams moves to assistant head coach after undergoing treatment for prostate cancer last season.
Drake Maye is the present and the future under center. He came up just short in the 2025 MVP race, with command far beyond most second-year quarterbacks. Maye can keep getting better, thanks to the additions of Brown and Romeo Doubs out wide. Should the passing game ever stall, Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson form a thunder-and-lightning duo on the ground. Henderson is listed as out for Wednesday, though, due to an ankle injury.
The top-line defense gets boosted by two big free-agency moves. Edge rusher Dre’Mont Jones can help squeeze the pocket. And safety Kevin Byard III, who just led the league with seven interceptions, now looms deep over the secondary.
The Patriots have an especially tough Week 1 draw. But winning in Seattle would send quite a message — to their competition and to themselves.
Seattle leads the regular-season head-to-head series 11-8. This is New England’s first game in front of the 12s since 2012. The Patriots visited Seattle in 2020, but the stadium was empty due to pandemic protocols.
The two teams have split their two postseason meetings. The Seahawks took a 19-0 lead early in the fourth quarter of February’s Super Bowl, en route to their decisive 29-13 win and their second championship. Walker earned MVP shine with 161 yards of offense. Hall and Murphy had two sacks apiece; Julian Love and Uchenna Nwosu each came down with an interception.
Eleven years before that, Super Bowl XLIX gave us an all-time finish, from Jermaine Kearse’s heavenly juggle to Malcolm Butler’s fateful pick at the goal line. Tom Brady took home the MVP honors after the Patriots’ 28-24 triumph, their fourth of what would become a six-ring dynasty.
The Seahawks are one of the many home teams favored in Week 1.

full_text:
How many wins will coach John Harbaugh and quarterback Jaxson Dart lead the Giants to in 2026? Julian Leshay Guadalupe / Imagn Images
Few people know coach John Harbaugh better than Mike Tomlin.
As coach of the Pittsburgh Steelers from 2007-25, Tomlin faced off against Harbaugh’s Baltimore Ravens 44 times, including four games in the postseason. For nearly two decades, they were the faces of one of the best rivalries the NFL had to offer.
But times have changed. Harbaugh is now the new face of the New York Giants, while Tomlin signed on as a studio analyst for NBC Sports’ Football Night in America. In preparation for his debut in that role, the man who knows what a Harbaugh football team looks like better than almost anybody outlined what Giants fans can expect from their new coach.
“Harbs definitively has a mode of operation,” Tomlin said ahead of the Giants’ game Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys. “He has a definitive style for how he engineers victory, and that’s a major component of winning and winning consistently.”
Tomlin added that he anticipates that style will take hold in New York immediately and that the Giants will be more competitive in 2026 than people might expect.
Tomlin isn’t alone in that opinion. In surveying analysts across the league, the national consensus appears to be that the Giants will be better than most people expect — thanks to Harbaugh.
“I say this without discrediting anything or anyone from before, but there is just an adult element in the building now,” ESPN’s Dan Orlovsky said. “I say this all the time, but it’s not just Sundays, and it’s not just the season. Harbaugh knows what February feels and sounds like. He knows what March feels and sounds like for teams that are good, competitive teams. He knows what you do post-draft in April. (He knows) what the OTAs are supposed to be (and) how sharp you’re supposed to be. (He knows) what a training camp is supposed to feel like for a team that’s a good football team. … Just being able to tap into the past is a really valuable asset that, honestly, not a lot of the coaches from beforehand had that (kind of) experience.”
For as much optimism as those who watch the league are expressing for the Giants this preseason, it’s tough to overstate how big of a hill Harbaugh has to climb to get this franchise back to being competitive. The Giants finished 4-13 last season and 3-14 in 2024. Their 13-38 record over the past three seasons is the second-worst mark in the NFL over that stretch.
Suffice it to say, Harbaugh’s task is daunting. And that leads us to a question we pose to our panel of national analysts every year around this time : What would be a successful season for the Giants? For a team that has won more than six games just once in the past decade, what bar does Harbaugh need to clear to make the future feel bright in New York?
Orlovsky defines success in Year 1 of the Harbaugh era as playing meaningful games into December. NFL Network analyst Brian Baldinger, however, thinks the Giants have what it takes to make the playoffs.
“Harbaugh is a great coach, and they’ve got very good talent,” Baldinger said. “So how they bring it together, and how they coach them, and how they figure out ways to win games, that’s the job of the coach and the staff. But they’ve got everything it takes to be one of the seven best teams in the NFC.”
Amazon Prime’s Andrew Whitworth didn’t forecast a playoff season for the Giants, but he also didn’t believe that needs to be the barometer for success; he simply wants to see signs of progress.
“There are enough questions there that, if I’m a Giants fan, I’m saying, ‘Listen, (our) defense has some really talented young players; we made some investments in our offensive line; we have a quarterback and a tailback now who are going to be healthy, and they gave us some positive play last year, so where can we build off of that?’ Whitworth said. “I mean, I’m a little excited to see where it goes.”
Unsurprisingly, Whitworth’s excitement about the Giants’ future stems from his days facing off with Harbaugh’s Ravens. The four-time Pro Bowl offensive tackle spent the first 11 seasons of his career playing for the Ravens’ AFC North rival Cincinnati Bengals, nine of which came against Harbaugh-led teams.
“I think even just looking at where they went in the draft, it’s very clear, Harbaugh didn’t lose his way,” said Whitworth, referring to the Giants’ selections of linebacker Arvell Reese at No. 5 overall and offensive lineman Francis Mauigoa at No. 10. “Every year, you knew you were going to play guys that look the part, if anything else. There’s going to be an emphasis (on) the physicality they play with, the way they execute. A special teams coach, and that’s what his background is, like that’s all in the fine details, and that’s what elite special teams are. I would imagine a really physical team that’s not going to beat itself.”
Baldinger also highlighted Harbaugh’s special teams background as an asset, saying he expects the group to be “special.” He also noted the emphasis on physicality and wanting to dominate the line of scrimmage, witnessing those things firsthand when he attended the Aug. 20 joint practice between the Giants and Dolphins in Miami.
One of the other biggest reasons for optimism about the Giants in 2026 comes with a massive caveat, according to Baldinger and Whitworth. While the Giants’ pass rush will be fearsome, thanks to Brian Burns, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux, the analysts have significant concerns about how much the Giants’ defense will allow the pass rush to matter. Specifically, they have real concerns about New York’s defensive tackle depth chart, which was already worth questioning even before the team traded Dexter Lawrence.
“The truth in the NFL is you got to earn your right to rush the passer, so it’s going to have to be earned by all those skillful rushers on first and second down,” Whitworth said. “How do they play against the run? Their ability to stop the run and play with some physicality, that’s gonna be a big key to the success of this Giants defense.”
On the offensive side of the ball, Orlovsky has three elements in particular he’ll be looking at when defining what a successful Giants season looks like. The first is whether the offensive line, consisting of four returners (left tackle Andrew Thomas, left guard Jon Runyan Jr., center John Michael Schmitz and right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor) and one rookie right guard, Mauigoa, can be the five of the future? He believes the unit has the makings of the best one the Giants have fielded in the last 10 years.
The next piece for Orlovsky is quarterback Jaxson Dart taking tangible steps forward in his second season in the league. For Orlovsky, that starts with cleaning up his footwork. Finally, Orlovsky also wants to see a better understanding of situational risk — with the football and when it comes to Dart’s sometimes unchecked aggression in the run game. As a rookie, Dart faced a lot of criticism for his tendency to take big hits as a runner. That’s been a major point of emphasis under the new coaching staff.
Unsurprisingly, Baldinger wants to see growth in that area, too.
“He’s got a better offensive line that he should trust to be able to stand back there and make his reads,” Baldinger said. “I don’t think he has to do as much as he did last year. I don’t think he should run as much as he did. He’s a good runner, so I don’t want to say he shouldn’t run. He can do that. I think he’s got to be more disciplined. We saw this in Year 2 from (Bears quarterback) Caleb Williams. He should be able to stand back there, five yards behind the center, seven yards behind the center, and go through whatever progressions there are to get it to an open receiver. I want to see that on a more consistent basis from him.
“I want to see him play the game with no fear, but with less running and less frenetic scrambling than he demonstrated a year ago.”

New Eagles offensive coordinator Sean Mannion has impressed Jalen Hurts and his teammates with his clear explanations and attention to detail. Mitchell Leff / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — Sean Mannion kept two playbooks as a backup quarterback. He studied the Vikings’ edition, which he needed to master as Kirk Cousins’ backup in Minnesota in 2023. Then, there was the binder full of plays he accumulated for the living playbook he designed for when he would eventually lead an offense.
The collection started early. Mannion’s home includes a framed yellow notepad on which he sketched plays as a 7-year-old at his father’s football practices. His college coach at Oregon State, Mike Riley, remembers a “monster video study” of passing concepts dating back seven decades.
So, when Chris Kuper, then a Vikings assistant and now the Philadelphia Eagles’ offensive line coach, fielded Mannion’s questions about protections in 2023, he recognized Mannion’s preparation as Cousins’ understudy. Those questions were also preparing Mannion for his current role: Eagles offensive coordinator.
“I figured he had an inkling that maybe it might be something he wants to do,” Kuper said, “and now we’re seeing it.”
Mannion’s first official game as an offensive coordinator is perhaps the most anticipated Eagles debut this weekend, given the stakes of the hire and the curiosity surrounding the 34-year-old. Coach Nick Sirianni needed a new offensive coordinator for the fifth consecutive season after the offense’s regression in 2025 prompted the biggest change of the Sirianni era.
The search initially focused on an experienced play-caller. It eventually led to an opposite profile: the former NFL quarterback with only two years of coaching experience and no NFL play-calling experience.
Much of the attention has focused on Mannion’s new scheme, with roots in the Sean McVay system. That was part of the appeal for Sirianni. But in the NFL, if you’re chasing a trend, you’re often late. Mannion’s success won’t be based primarily on scheme. It will depend on a football mind cultivated long before he became a coach. McVay’s luster is not necessarily about his playbook, but his brilliance in implementing it.
That’s what the Eagles are beginning to witness.
“If I were to lock the three smartest people in the facility in one room, Sean would be there,” offensive tackle Jordan Mailata said, “and I think Sean will just be by himself.”
Mannion’s “born-to-coach” narrative belies how he’s long been known in football circles. When you’re a 6-foot-6, 230-pound, four-year starting quarterback in the Pac-12 with more than 13,600 passing yards and 83 touchdowns in the profile, coaching can wait.
Mannion wasn’t making airport runs in his early 20s while working the grunt job of a low-level staffer. Yes, Riley saw coaching in Mannion’s future. But Mannion was busy throwing for 481 yards and four touchdowns against Cal (and eventual No. 1 pick Jared Goff). The focus then was on the Saturday game plan.
It’s why the distinction between man and scheme matters. The football mind was apparent during weekly preparation and the quick processing on the field at Oregon State. Mannion made adjustments with eventual first-round pick Brandin Cooks in between plays based on the defense’s presentation. He consumed the game plans — “Nobody surpassed him,” said Riley, who coached multiple NFL quarterbacks in Corvallis, Ore. — and banked what resonated with him.
“This is what I think is important in coaching — to have a diverse background in what people do,” Riley said. “And then you have to be selective in what you’re going to do. Through study, coaches come up with or select a group of things that they like. But you have to have an inventory behind them, and that’s what Sean was doing.”
Mannion was a 2015 third-round pick by the St. Louis Rams and joined a quarterback room with Nick Foles as a rookie. Before his second season, the Rams traded for the No. 1 pick and drafted Goff. The 2017 season was transformative for Mannion. It wasn’t because of how he played, although Hall of Famer Eric Dickerson said during a pre-training camp interview that the Rams should start Mannion over Goff. It was his exposure to McVay, along with an offensive staff that included future NFL head coaches Matt LaFleur and Zac Taylor.
“I just felt like I was learning so, so much,” Mannion said. “It was such an exciting way to match the run and pass. They had such a way about teaching the game where we could feel ourselves challenging a defense, but it felt simple to us. Those are the things that really stood out to me going through that experience that really resonated with me as a player and certainly resonated with me as a coach. That was a very exciting point in my football life, just the exposure to that type of teaching, that type of scheme.”
He soon began the journeyman life of an NFL backup, bouncing between Minnesota and Seattle from 2019 to 2023. He was exposed to offensive minds with head coaching jobs on their resumes, including Gary Kubiak, Kevin O’Connell, Kevin Stefanski, Klint Kubiak and Dave Canales, plus a number of future offensive coordinators.
Mannion transitioned from potential starter to veteran backup, offering answers and support in the meeting room, seeing the game through the starters’ eyes. Kind of like a coach. Those years became an incubator of offensive ideas, pulling leaves from different branches of the scheme and adding plays and ideas to the binder that would soon blossom in Philadelphia.
“Very, very obvious early on that he was going to be a coach the minute he decided he was going to stop playing,” said Stefanski, who was Mannion’s offensive coordinator in 2019. “I think great coaches come from that (backup) role because you have to prepare yourself to play, even when you’re not getting the reps. So, I think he’s been really developed into it. … Developed by the different stops that he’s had, by the different people that he’s had. But it’s always been in him to coach.”
Mannion moved from the quarterback depth chart to a coach’s office, joining Green Bay’s staff in 2024 and working under LaFleur. He was promoted to quarterbacks coach after one season, tasked with preparing both Jordan Love and Malik Willis to win games. It’s an example of adjusting to personnel and flexibility within a scheme, molding to players as Mannion is expected to do in Philadelphia. The Packers did not want to lose him.
“Not shocked that it happened that fast because of the way he works,” Packers general manager Brian Gutekunst said. “Usually when you bring in a young, really talented coach, you’re kind of hoping to have him for a number of years, and that’s unfortunate for us, but he’s going to do a great job. The ability to see the game through a quarterback’s eyes because of his playing career, coming from a coaching family, there’s just a lot to like there.”
Mailata left his first meeting with Mannion calling his new offensive coordinator an “evil genius,” fitting the profile of the wunderkind play-callers who have become vogue around the NFL.
Part of it might have been the scheme change — “It’s basically been the same offense every year. This is different,” defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said — but it went beyond new concepts such as more under-center plays and the wide-zone running scheme.
What mattered to Mailata was how Mannion explained it.
“I think when we’re being taught the scheme, just the explanation of how the defense is going to see it and what the plan is,” Mailata said. “You see it, and you’re like, ‘That’s actually pretty smart, why didn’t I think about that?’ … You may not understand it at the time, and then you go through the meetings, and he breaks down everything. There’s a purpose to everything in the plan. You see the defense kind of confused — who’s covering who in this motion, how does that affect the D-line and O-line, the run sell.”

full_text:
After an impressive preseason, Germie Bernard makes his NFL regular-season debut on Sunday. Charles LeClaire / Imagn Images
PITTSBURGH — Shortly after Germie Bernard arrived at training camp in Latrobe, Aaron Rodgers pulled the rookie receiver off to the side. In no uncertain terms, the future Hall of Fame quarterback laid out his expectations.
“If you want to be able to play with me, these are the things that you need to know,” Bernard remembers Rodgers telling him. “You need to learn how to think like this. You need to know what to do after this. You need to know what to think in these circumstances.”
A self-described perfectionist, Rodgers has a detailed and demanding approach that is part of why he’s won four MVPs and a Super Bowl. It’s also why young receivers have sometimes struggled to make an impact. Davante Adams felt some of that early in his Green Bay days. Roman Wilson absorbed it often last year, as he tumbled down the Steelers’ depth chart and, eventually, off the game-day roster.
Rodgers expects receivers to be where they’re supposed to be when they’re supposed to be there. In a true West Coast offense, the depths of the receivers’ routes are married to the steps of a QB’s drops. Rodgers explained this offseason that a QB should be able to throw the ball blindfolded.
“It’s really made me home in (on) the smallest details,” Bernard said. “He’s very detail-oriented. It made me dive deeper into my playbook, dive deeper into my relationship with him, so I can start to understand the way that he thinks.”
A versatile receiver, Bernard has the skill set to line up at all three positions: X, Y and Z. The Steelers have asked him to learn all three positions so he can move seamlessly around the offense. However, getting on the field early goes beyond just knowing the plays in the playbook.
Coach Mike McCarthy said this week the team isn’t going to have a “black-and-white, run-it offense.” They’re going to lean into their quarterback’s experience and give him plenty of latitude to get the team into the right plays at the line of scrimmage. For Bernard, that means deciphering hand signals, being prepared to run the second or third play that’s called in the huddle and adjusting routes on the fly based on coverages.
“There’s a big difference between trusting a guy and then knowing if he’s ready in big situations,” Rodgers said. “It’s a process. I think it’s the mental part first. We challenge them in some of the periods that we do with some quick thinking and adjustments and coverage on the fly. You’ve got to see how they react to it. He’s got a great attitude. He works really hard. He cares about it and puts in the time.”
During the preseason, Bernard began to show how his skill set can translate to a McCarthy-Rodgers offense. Offenses with West Coast roots emphasize getting the ball to playmakers, stressing defenses horizontally and creating yards after the catch. At nearly 6-2 and 205 pounds, Bernard is rugged and can be a handful to bring down in the open field. Of his 64 receiving yards, 46 of them came after the catch. He was often running through arm tackles, including on a catch-and-run touchdown against the Bills. It mirrors his college production. At Alabama last year, he forced 17 missed tackles.
“Aaron Rodgers always says, ‘Know who you are. Know your strengths,'” Bernard said. “When you’re watching tape, you can look for those opportunities. I know what my strengths are, so when I get those opportunities I turn those into a positive.”
While it can be a challenge for any receiver to adapt to Rodgers’ perfectionist approach, Bernard’s background could help ease this transition. Drafted in the second round, he was considered a pro-ready prospect after two full years as a starter at Alabama, plus half a season in a starting role at Washington. In Dane Brugler’s draft profile, scouts praised Bernard for his professional and mature approach to the game.
“(Bernard) owned that receiver room and is popular in the program,” one NFL scout told Brugler .
That attitude has shone through early on. With a naturally joyful personality and an ever-present smile, Bernard carries himself with confidence and isn’t afraid to ask for advice. He sees the bigger picture and realizes that having a veteran of 20-plus seasons as his QB is only going to benefit him in the long run.
“I want to ask as many questions as I can,” Bernard said. “I want to learn as much as I can. I’m always just being a sponge. For (Rodgers) to trust me and really coach me, it’s been nothing but great. I’m really glad that I’m able to have a healthy relationship with him. It means a lot to me, because not everybody has that privilege of being under a Hall of Fame QB.”
As Bernard prepares for his NFL debut on Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons, coaches have been careful not to ask too much of the rookie too soon. Bernard is currently listed as the fourth receiver on the depth chart, behind DK Metcalf, Michael Pittman Jr. and Wilson. However, as the season unfolds, Bernard could challenge Wilson for the slot receiver role in 11 personnel (three-receiver) packages.
Make no mistake: The Steelers will certainly tap into Bernard’s skill set as early as this week. Earning a bigger piece of the pie starts with building his relationship with Rodgers.
“The biggest thing for me is I know that he wants guys out there that he can trust,” Bernard said. “No one is going to be perfect. When you make a mistake, can you fix it and not make it again? I focus on all the little critiques, all the little details that he’s telling me so when I have that same play or the same route, I’m not making the same mistake.”

full_text:
Sam Darnold's Seahawks beat the Rams in two out of three meetings last season, including in the NFC Championship Game. Jane Gershovich / Getty Images
RENTON, Wash. — Rest assured, all is well with Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold’s Super Bowl ring.
During the Seahawks’ ring ceremony in June, Darnold dropped his , but it emerged from the short fall unscathed.
“Of course this would happen to me, dropping the ring,” Darnold said Monday. “But I will say in my defense. … I opened the box, and the ring was already falling out. It wasn’t like I made the ring fall out of the box. I just wanted to clear that up.”
Likewise, the Seahawks want to make it abundantly obvious that they have no intention of living in the past. Seattle begins its title defense on Wednesday with a Super Bowl rematch against the New England Patriots in both teams’ season opener at Lumen Field.
Thanks to a family member with plenty of expertise on the matter, veteran defensive lineman Leonard Williams knows a tough task awaits the Seahawks. They hope to become the ninth franchise in NFL history to win back-to-back Super Bowls.
Williams’ father-in-law is Hall of Fame safety Ronnie Lott, who secured consecutive Super Bowl titles (plus two others) with the San Francisco 49ers in 1989 and 1990.
“He talked about how hard it is to repeat,” Williams said. “That was part of what he told me that’s hard about it: Guys look to the last season instead of looking forward, and we’re not doing that around here.”
Nor are the Seahawks getting googly-eyed about all the hype surrounding the Los Angeles Rams, either. Los Angeles is the clear favorite to win the Super Bowl with +500 odds. This year features the largest preseason gap between the top two teams in Super Bowl odds since the 2017 Patriots (+275) opened as favorites over the Seahawks, Green Bay Packers and Las Vegas Raiders (all +800). Seattle is tied for fourth in preseason odds at +1200, behind the Rams, Buffalo Bills and Baltimore Ravens (both +1000).
The Rams, who finished runner-up to the Seahawks in the NFC last year, added reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett, cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson and coaxed three-time DPOY Aaron Donald out of retirement. Seahawks safety Julian Love admitted it would be naive to say he has not paid attention to the Rams’ latest additions.
“But at the same time, I feel like, ‘How can we let that affect anything we do right now?’ is kind of the mindset,” Love said of the Rams. “We play those guys in December at some point. It’s September. It’s that mindset of, ‘We have more things to worry about.’ The biggest fish to fry is the one that’s right in front of us, and that’s New England.”
To Love’s point, the Seahawks won’t see the Rams until Christmas Day in Seattle. The teams will meet again two weeks later for the regular-season finale in Los Angeles. In the meantime, the Seahawks have been busy getting adjusted to first-year offensive coordinator Brian Fleury’s system ahead of Wednesday’s season opener.
Backup quarterback Drew Lock said the praise for the high-flying Rams hasn’t come up a lot in Seattle’s locker room. That’s not because the team is seeking to avoid the topic; rather, there just isn’t much time for those kinds of discussions.
“If I was in Sam’s shoes, I wouldn’t be going home thinking about what people are necessarily saying,” Lock said of Darnold. “I’d be thinking about what my kid’s eating for dinner, and is he actually going to eat it, or is he going to throw it on the ground?”
It helps, too, that the Seahawks would like to avoid being satisfied. Linebacker Ernest Jones IV said complacency would be Seattle’s pitfall, should the team fall short of expectations in 2026, a sentiment Williams echoed.
“You can win it all and just think you’ve got it all figured out,” Jones said. “The other 31 teams are evolving, and they’re trying to get better. They’re trying to get to where you are.”
With the way the Rams retooled their roster, they might have a deeper squad on paper than Seattle. But the Seahawks return reigning Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba, all five starting offensive linemen and many key contributors from the “Dark Side,” Seattle’s vaunted defense that allowed the fewest points per game in the league last season.
Having a sparkling recent track record doesn’t hurt Seattle’s cause, either, especially when it comes to winning over players like Love. The first three years of the safety’s career were spent on New York Giants teams that posted sub-.500 records.
“Success accelerates trusting the process,” Love said. “I’ve been in some places where you lose some games or some things go left, and you’re like, ‘Man, this process isn’t working.’ And so, it’s very easy for us to trust the process because we had success last year. We just feel good about how we go about work each day. We know nobody’s short-cutting anything.”
Still, it will be a challenge for Seattle to defend its crown, and not simply because one of its division rivals is the favorite to win it all. Williams expects the Seahawks to receive their opponents’ best each week.
In the process, Williams hopes Seattle can forge a new identity. The Seahawks will have their first opportunity to do so Wednesday.
Then, in due time, they can shift their attention to the Rams — regardless of whether they’re duking it out for a spot in the Super Bowl.
“Coming off of a successful year, we’re not trying to chase the previous team that we once were,” Williams said. “Even though that was just a year ago or months ago, we understand that it’s a whole new season and whole new team.”

full_text:
Drake Maye's Pats are off to the Emerald City, seeking revenge for their Super Bowl loss. Mark J. Rebilas / Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
The NFL’s newest season begins where its last one left off — with the New England Patriots, Seattle Seahawks and National Broadcasting Company.
A Super Bowl LX rematch is here to officially kick off the 2026 NFL campaign. No, Bad Bunny won’t be performing in the middle of this one, but there’s so much to look forward to in the season opener. The Seahawks raise their championship banner before the euphoric 12s. The Patriots seek revenge after February’s frustrating loss. It’s “Sunday Night Football” on a friggin’ Wednesday .
We’re all reporting as eligible tonight. Here’s what we can expect to see and hear from game No. 1 of 272.
NBC is free over the air. It’s also available with Peacock’s premium plan.
This is the third Week 1 to feature a Super Bowl rematch. It last happened in 2016, when the Denver Broncos beat the Carolina Panthers. This is the second time that an NFL season opens on a Wednesday — the Dallas Cowboys and New York Giants did it in 2012.
NBC has aired the season opener for more than two consecutive decades. The 2026 edition puts Mike Tirico on play-by-play and Cris Collinsworth on analyst duties. Melissa Stark and Kaylee Hartung are the corresponding field reporters. They were all on the call for Super Bowl LX, too.
There’s a pregame program called “NFL Kickoff Special.” It starts at 7 p.m. ET and is hosted by Maria Taylor. New Englanders will certainly recognize Devin McCourty, a 13-year defensive back for the Pats and a three-time Super Bowl champ . Everyone will recognize Mike Tomlin as he goes from unblinking head coach to studio staple. The desk also has NFL insider Mike Florio and enthusiastic clapper Jason Garrett.
Mike Macdonald’s Hawks were a two-way torpedo throughout 2025. They finished with the No. 3 scoring offense, No. 1 scoring defense and top seed in their conference. Despite a few offseason departures and the NFL’s ephemerality, Seattle takes the field as a viable back-to-back champ.
Kenneth Walker III is no longer in the backfield after signing with the Kansas City Chiefs. New Zealand native George Holani and Notre Dame draftee Jadarian Price will carry the load while last year’s RB2, Zach Charbonnet, recovers from knee surgery. The offense also replaces coordinator Klint Kubiak, who is now head coach of the Las Vegas Raiders. His successor, Brian Fleury, was tight ends coach and run game coordinator for the rival San Francisco 49ers.
Sam Darnold is back as QB1 and lead bird watcher . Jaxon Smith-Njigba is the reigning Offensive Player of the Year, looking to defend his receiving title amid double coverage. His presence frees up room for the steady Cooper Kupp and turbo-booster Rashid Shaheed.
The “ Dark Side ” defense boasts a disciplined front line and a secondary that can stuff the run. DL Leonard Williams and CB Devon Witherspoon are both fresh off of well-earned contract extensions. Derick Hall and Byron Murphy II return to the loaded pass rush; second-team All-Pro Ernest Jones IV holds down the second level. Newly signed defensive back Terrion Arnold won’t play in Week 1 as he remains on the commissioner’s exempt list while facing kidnapping and armed robbery charges.
Wednesday night begins an extended curtain call for sack artist DeMarcus Lawrence as well. The 13-year pro says that he will retire at the end of the season.
Like their opponents, the Patriots put together a dominant 2025. They went 14-3, ranking second in points scored and fourth in points allowed.
Then came an intense offseason. Coach of the Year Mike Vrabel was caught up in a scandal with Dianna Russini, who at the time was The Athletic ’s NFL insider . In June, the front office made a trade for A.J. Brown , one of the league’s best and most emotive players . There was also a protracted contract dispute with lockdown corner Christian Gonzalez, who received a record extension days before the start of the season.
On the sideline, Vrabel and offensive play caller Josh McDaniels are still at their posts. Zak Kuhr officially shifts from inside linebackers coach to defensive coordinator, while former DC Terrell Williams moves to assistant head coach after undergoing treatment for prostate cancer last season.
Drake Maye is the present and the future under center. He came up just short in the 2025 MVP race, with command far beyond most second-year quarterbacks. Maye can keep getting better, thanks to the additions of Brown and Romeo Doubs out wide. Should the passing game ever stall, Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson form a thunder-and-lightning duo on the ground. Henderson is listed as out for Wednesday, though, due to an ankle injury.
The top-line defense gets boosted by two big free-agency moves. Edge rusher Dre’Mont Jones can help squeeze the pocket. And safety Kevin Byard III, who just led the league with seven interceptions, now looms deep over the secondary.
The Patriots have an especially tough Week 1 draw. But winning in Seattle would send quite a message — to their competition and to themselves.
Seattle leads the regular-season head-to-head series 11-8. This is New England’s first game in front of the 12s since 2012. The Patriots visited Seattle in 2020, but the stadium was empty due to pandemic protocols.
The two teams have split their two postseason meetings. The Seahawks took a 19-0 lead early in the fourth quarter of February’s Super Bowl, en route to their decisive 29-13 win and their second championship. Walker earned MVP shine with 161 yards of offense. Hall and Murphy had two sacks apiece; Julian Love and Uchenna Nwosu each came down with an interception.
Eleven years before that, Super Bowl XLIX gave us an all-time finish, from Jermaine Kearse’s heavenly juggle to Malcolm Butler’s fateful pick at the goal line. Tom Brady took home the MVP honors after the Patriots’ 28-24 triumph, their fourth of what would become a six-ring dynasty.
The Seahawks are one of the many home teams favored in Week 1.

MELBOURNE, Australia — Mike Evans was trying to downplay it, and he even started muttering the old cliché about how every game is important. But then he stopped himself.
“It’s in Australia … the first game of the season … my first game with this team … division opponent,” the 49ers receiver reminded himself. “Yeah, I guess there is a little bit extra juice. For sure.”
With all the talk surrounding the Los Angeles Rams’ trading for pass rusher deluxe Myles Garrett and bringing Aaron Donald out of retirement, 49ers players clear their throats when talking about the signing of Evans, who had 11 straight 1,000-yard seasons for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
“You can’t put a cornerback on him one-on-one, so that will open things up for everyone else on our offense,” tight end George Kittle said.
George Kittle says Mike Evans needs no coaching points: pic.twitter.com/fovjZSk04b
— Vic Tafur (@VicTafur) September 9, 2026
The 6-foot-5 Evans is the first true X receiver coach Kyle Shanahan has had since his days with Julio Jones winning one-on-one matchups in Atlanta. “He’s a stud,” Shanahan said before Wednesday’s practice.
Quarterback Brock Purdy and left tackle Trent Williams were also giddy about the acquisition of the likely Hall of Famer, and he has not disappointed.
“He’s a gold-jacket player, and it’s kind of what you expect,” Williams said. “We ain’t seen nothing less whenever he’s been on the field. It’s been cool having him around — just another veteran presence, another guy that’s a household name, done this for a long, long time at a very high level.
“Just having him around for this young locker room has been valuable.”
Evans has taken De’Zhaun Stribling under his wing and has been impressed every step of the way as the rookie has taken on a larger role after Ricky Pearsall needed season-ending surgery.
“He’s gonna be a great player, and he’s gonna help us out a lot this year,” Evans said. “He’s the ultimate playmaker. He’s physical, he’s tough, has great hands, and he’s really smart and is low-maintenance.”
Evans, 33, prides himself on being low-maintenance, though he chuckles that maybe he wasn’t as a younger player. He wanted to play for a Super Bowl contender, left home for less money to do it and has never looked back.
Evans walked into the 49ers locker room, with a lot of veteran leaders, and has fit in well.
“There’s a lot of people with a voice, and they lead by example,” Evans said. “And I’m happy I get to add my experience as well.
“I had to get a feel for everyone and kind of say, ‘This is who I am,’ but everyone’s been receptive and super positive. It’s been a cool transition.”
Evans said the team has a lot of confidence after a “super competitive camp.” He missed some time with groin and quad injuries but said he is not concerned and wouldn’t have missed any time if it were the regular season.
“The training staff, they did a great job working with me,” Evans said. “I know I’m an older player. I’ve had probably over a thousand … football practices in my life now, so I know what I’m doing out there. They know what they’re doing.”
Offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said Evans’ veteran presence is clear.
“He’s seen a lot of football, and he’s a very savvy, confident veteran football player who adds a lot of leadership qualities to our room. And he’s a matchup issue,” Kubiak said. “And what I’ve been most impressed about Mike is Mike doesn’t ask a lot of questions. He doesn’t overthink a lot of things.
“‘Give me the route, tell me the play; I’m going to find a way to get it done.’”
“We’re going to be able to say that we were the first team to play in Australia,” Evans said. “And that’s cool.”
It’s the farthest Evans has flown since his honeymoon in Tahiti 10 years ago. But he has loved everything about it.
“I thought the flight was gonna be extremely hard, but it was easy, you know,” Evans said. “We had fun on the flight. We got good rest.”
Bring on the Rams, and bring on the 100,000 fans.
“That will give us some extra juice going,” Evans said.

full_text:
Last year's No. 1 pick approaches Year No. 2 in Nashville. Johnnie Izquierdo / Getty Images
The Tennessee Titans finished 3-14 for the second consecutive season in 2025. Brian Callahan was fired after six games, and an offense that never found much traction finished 30th in scoring. No. 1 pick Cam Ward was sacked 55 times, tied for a league high, in his 17 starts as the Titans struggled to give him much help.
Robert Saleh arrives in Tennessee after spending 2025 as defensive coordinator for the San Francisco 49ers, returning to a head-coaching role after nearly four seasons leading the New York Jets. He brings with him a largely new staff. Brian Daboll will run the offense and Gus Bradley the defense, while John Fassel is back as special teams coordinator.
Year 2 should provide a much clearer read on Ward now. He threw for 3,169 yards, 15 touchdowns and seven interceptions as a rookie, improving late before injuring his right shoulder in the season finale. He’s healthy again and has a significantly upgraded supporting cast. At receiver, the Titans signed Wan’Dale Robinson and used the No. 4 overall pick on Ohio State’s Carnell Tate. Calvin Ridley returns out wide, while running back Tony Pollard is coming off a career year in which he rushed for 1,082 yards.
Tennessee also reshaped its defense this offseason. The Titans traded for edge rusher Jermaine Johnson II, who was a Pro Bowler under Saleh in 2023. They signed defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers and cornerbacks Alontae Taylor and Cor’Dale Flott, then used the No. 31 pick on Auburn edge rusher Keldric Faulk and a second-round pick on Texas linebacker Anthony Hill Jr.
Watching the Titans this season is relatively straightforward. Tennessee’s first 16 games are Sunday afternoon matchups split between CBS and Fox. Only the Week 18 trip to face the Houston Texans remains TBD. Saleh’s tenure with the Titans opens at home against his former Jets team.
Be sure to follow the Titans on The Athletic , along with national NFL coverage from “ The Athletic Football Show ” and Scoop City , throughout the season.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
The Titans are currently scheduled to appear 10 times on CBS this season. Their Week 17 matchup with the Pittsburgh Steelers will be the final regular-season game at the current Nissan Stadium.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables .…

full_text:
Dan Quinn and the Washington Commanders face a crucial opening stretch of the 2026 season. Tommy Gilligan / Imagn Images
We’ve reviewed the concerns along the offensive line . We know how little the starters played in three preseason games. We know there are banged-up players along the defensive front. And we understand that Jayden Daniels’ play and Jayden Daniels’ health probably matter more than any of it.
But with the Washington Commanders finally, mercifully arriving at a practice week that ends with a regular-season game, there are a few less frequently discussed issues that could have an enormous impact on the season. Let’s get at them:
General manager Adam Peters had this to say about Sunday’s opener at Philadelphia:
“We couldn’t be more thrilled than to start our season where we’re starting it,” Peters said after he and coach Dan Quinn finalized their third roster together. “It’s gonna be a great challenge, and we’re looking forward to it.”
Might be an odd way to think about playing an Eagles franchise that has won back-to-back NFC East titles and been to the playoffs in all five seasons of coach Nick Sirianni’s tenure. But if Washington’s season is going to be a success — and a success means returning to the playoffs after last year’s 5-12 disaster — then it says here the Commanders are going to have to figure out a way to win at least one of their first two games, which are at Philly and at Dallas.
Consider that in the last 20 NFL seasons, only 65 teams have opened with back-to-back divisional games. Of those teams, just 10 went 0-2. Of that group, just one — last year’s Chicago Bears — managed to put behind the miserable start against its biggest rivals and reach the playoffs.
Even more ominous: Of those 10 teams to start 0-2 with both losses coming against divisional opponents, five fired their coaches, four in midseason: the 2019 Washington team (Jay Gruden after an 0-5 start), the 2020 Detroit Lions (Matt Patricia after a 4-7 start), the 2023 Carolina Panthers (Frank Reich after a 1-10 start), the 2025 New York Giants (Brian Daboll after a 2-8 start) and the 2025 Cleveland Browns (Kevin Stefanski after the season). Another one of those teams, the 2017 Browns, went 0-16.
The schedule doesn’t get much easier in the first half: Five of the Commanders’ first eight games come against 2025 playoff teams, including the home opener against the Super Bowl champion Seahawks in Week 3. The second half — with just two playoff teams (Houston and Jacksonville) in nine games — might provide a chance to go on a run. But it’s almost impossible to see having success within the division without beating either the Eagles or the Cowboys in September.
A year ago, Blough was an assistant quarterbacks coach, just two seasons removed from a five-year career as a backup and practice squad quarterback who lost all seven starts he made as a pro. Now, he is not only the offensive coordinator given the keys to a new system with Daniels at the helm, but he’s also been allowed to build that system from the ground up.
If the premise is that for the Commanders to excel, Daniels needs to excel — and that’s a pretty foolproof premise — then Blough’s ability to keep his quarterback out of danger and maximize his extraordinary abilities is paramount.
Blough, 31, played under former Commanders’ offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury when Kingsbury served as the head coach of the Arizona Cardinals. But his charge has been to construct a system that differs from Kingsbury’s in almost every way. Kingsbury’s offense rarely huddled; Blough’s will, unless time is ticking down. Kingsbury’s offense rarely moved receivers around or put skill position players in motion; Blough’s will do both on a high percentage of snaps.
And perhaps most important: Blough’s offense will rarely call a play that is designed for Daniels to run. Of all the numbers that explain why the Commanders struggled last season, none is more important than the fact that Daniels started and finished only four games. Daniels and Blough must join forces not only to make the offense more explosive, but to make sure it properly protects Daniels in both concepts and play calling.
Quick, name the seven men who have attempted at least one field goal or extra point for the Commanders over the previous two seasons. Obsessive fans only need apply. (Answer below.)
When Washington plays at Philadelphia, Drew Stevens will almost certainly become the eighth. The undrafted rookie from Iowa easily beat out veteran Jake Moody in training camp. The Commanders elected to cut Moody after the first preseason game — a game in which Moody clanked a 29-yarder off the upright and through and Stevens drilled his only attempt, from 41 yards. Stevens was also the more consistent kicker throughout camp, making 43 of 48 attempts from all distances at the time Moody was released, as opposed to Moody’s 36-of-47 performance.
Stevens clearly had the stronger leg. But he is also hardly infallible. In the preseason finale at Baltimore, he was asked to attempt a 62-yarder — not a rarity in today’s NFL. He missed badly, both short and wide. It’s also worth noting that Stevens’s senior year at Iowa featured three missed kicks between 30 and 49 yards, exactly the kind of inconsistency that could lead an NFL team to look elsewhere — again.
(Answer: Moody, Matt Gay and Matthew Wright in 2025, Austin Seibert, Zane Gonzalez, Greg Joseph and Cade York in 2024.)
Another quiz: In the Peters-Quinn era of 2024-25, who leads the Commanders in rushing yards, attempts and average yards per carry?
That one should be easy, right? Jayden Daniels, who ran the ball — either by design or necessity — 206 times for 1,169 yards (a 5.7-yard clip) over his first two seasons.
That works out to 8.7 times a game as a rookie and 8.3 times per game last season.
That frequency has to stop. Which means the running game will fall to Jacory Croskey-Merritt, Rachaad White and Kaytron Allen (at least until Jeremy McNichols returns from injured reserve). That trio consists, respectively, of a seventh-round draft pick from 2025; a veteran who hasn’t averaged more than 4.3 yards per carry and is on a one-year, $2 million deal; and a rookie drafted in the sixth round this past spring.
Is that enough? The Commanders actually ran the ball fairly effectively in 2025, ranking fourth in the league in yards per game and fifth in yards per attempt. But 1,478 of their 2,290 yards on the ground last season came from players who are either on IR (McNichols), no longer play in Washington (Chris Rodriguez, Deebo Samuel, Austin Ekeler, Chris Moore), play quarterback (Daniels, Marcus Mariota) or some combination of those factors (Josh Johnson).
Croskey-Merritt is coming off a rookie season in which he ran for a team-high 805 yards and became a fan favorite. But he was banged up during most of training camp and didn’t appear in a preseason game.
White, who spent his first four seasons with Tampa Bay, appears to be Washington’s preferred option as a pass catcher out of the backfield, but he dealt with a hamstring issue during training camp and also didn’t appear in a game.
No one gained more rushing yards in the history of Penn State football than Allen, who ran for 85 yards in his preseason debut but fumbled on the Commanders’ first play from scrimmage in the finale against Baltimore.

title: Cardinals Bench Former First-Round Pick, Plus More Surprises on Depth Chart
full_text:
Darius Robinson is no longer a starter.
According to the team's first depth chart, the Arizona Cardinals have benched the former first-round pick in favor of Dante Stills.
It's a move we called earlier last week , though still a bit surprising given Robinson's status as a first-round pick entering his third season.
Robinson has largely failed to live up to the billing as a defensive lineman — practically every training camp is full of highlights of Robinson living in the backfield, though preseason and regular season have been a different story.
Perhaps that's unfair to Robinson, who dealt with early injuries and off-field loss during his rookie season. Or maybe this is a vote of confidence in Stills, who has largely been one of the more consistent players in the trenches. Hopefully next is a contract extension .
Robinson is built like a Greek statue and surely still has something to offer, though ahead of his third season, the Cardinals sent a clear message to the former top pick by placing Stills ahead of him.
Other notable depth chart moves:
Williams made a surprisingly early return from his Achilles injury, being activated from the PUP list and practicing with the Cardinals in the last few weeks. However, Arizona listed Williams behind all of Max Melton, Will Johnson and Denzel Burke.
This is presumably due to health, as the Cardinals may want to ease Williams back into action. Arizona chose not to have him remain on PUP, which in turn would have seen him miss the first four games of the season.
This could be another case of the Cardinals just wanting to ease players returning from injury to action.
Love suffered a high ankle sprain during preseason and hasn't fully practiced with the team in weeks. Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur was optimistic on Love playing this week, though it's clear Allgeier will shoulder much of the workload to begin the season.
It's very likely Gibbens and Simon will both play, as LaFleur said their utilization will heavily depend on what the game plan is on the week. However, it's interesting to note Simon was logging majority of first team reps through majority of the offseason before Gibbens arrived strong at the end.
It was enough to convince the Cardinals he's the starter — at least this week. Arizona now has a pair of athletic linebackers who can drop into coverage in Gibbens and Mack Wilson Sr.
Oftentimes teams will place "or" between two players to signify both are capable as starters and it simply depends on the week. With that established, there's only one "or" on the Cardinals' depth chart  (there were four on their final preseason depth chart).
That belongs at outside linebacker between Zaven Collins and Baron Browning. Collins is traditionally more suited to stop the run while Browning is their go-to option opposite Josh Sweat on obvious passing downs.

title: 7 Biggest Questions the Cardinals Must Answer Before Week 1
full_text:
It's football season in the desert.
The Arizona Cardinals are ramping up preparation for their Week 1 battle at SoFi Stadium with the Los Angeles Chargers.
The offseason is officially a thing of the past – it's go-time for the Cardinals, where wins and losses will count.
Seven of the biggest questions the Cardinals need to answer before Week 1 arrives:
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur is confident Jeremiyah Love will play in Week 1 — but how much?
Love is nursing a high ankle sprain suffered in preseason action and hasn't practiced since, so even if the Cardinals do rule him active for this week, it's more of a question of how much he'll play and how impactful he'll be.
If he's at 100% and fully recovered, that gives the Cardinals a weapon capable of explosive plays on the ground and through the air. Tyler Allgeier is a fine alternative lead back, though there's simply a different dynamic when Love is in the game.
This isn't being talked about enough, as Brissett was playing catch-up to learning LaFleur's offense this summer after lacking on-field reps thanks to his contract holdout. Brissett ultimately got what he wanted, but the work quickly began on getting him caught up to speed.
The Cardinals weren't worried about Brissett's ability to grasp LaFleur's offense thanks to his vast experience around the league. However, Brissett hadn't worked in the exact system LaFleur himself was installing in Arizona until his holdout ended in training camp.
Is Brissett fully caught up? Can the Cardinals run their full offense right out of the gate? Brissett's knowledge and confidence in owning the playbook could play a big factor on what Arizona's able to do.
The talk of the town lately has been Michael Wilson after his deserved contract extension while Trey McBride is a star in his own right at the tight end position. The Cardinals' offense should be fun, though we're most curious to see how Marvin Harrison Jr. is able to bounce back.
Harrison's two-year start to his NFL career has been full of ups and downs, though many were excited to see LaFleur hired thanks to his track record tied to receiver success in prior stops in Los Angeles and San Francisco.
If anybody can get the most out of the No. 4 overall pick, it feels like LaFleur — which sets the table for a massively important season in the desert. Harrison is obviously talented, and we're excited to see how he's deployed in an offense that should be receiver friendly over the course of the season.
There's supreme confidence in three of the Cardinals' starting five spots along the offensive line, all coming at LT, LG and C. Meanwhile, the entire right side of the offensive line is a massive question mark.
Arizona attempted to improve right guard with their second-round pick in Chase Bisontis, though that ultimately fell short thanks to an MCL injury that's set to keep him out for most (if not all) of 2026. Rather, Isaiah Adams has a clear path at the position to be a full-time starter.
At right tackle, Elijah Wilkinson was signed this offseason after a 2025 stint with the Atlanta Falcons where he led the team in sacks, pressures and penalties. He fits what the Cardinals want to do in terms of running the ball — but can he make strides in pass protection?
If both Adams and Wilkinson can raise their level of play, the Cardinals should be in business. If not? Arizona's gameplan could quickly be thrown out the window.
Josh Sweat didn't practice with the Cardinals at all until the week of their final preseason game, nursing his knee ahead of the 2026 regular season. Between his activation and game day in Los Angeles, Sweat will have had a few weeks to ramp up to game shape after missing every practice of OTAs, mandatory minicamp and training camp.
The knee isn't a concern here — the Cardinals put that bad boy in bubble wrap and made sure he'll be good to go. But what's Sweat's conditioning like? Will he be ready to play a full slate of snaps against the Chargers?
The Cardinals need Sweat to do some heavy lifting in terms of sack production. Arizona insisted he would be ready for the start of the season — but if Sweat needs to be on a snap count, then what was the point of having him miss practice all through the summer?
Inside linebacker was one of Arizona's more debated position battles this summer, though there doesn't appear to be a true winner at the other spot next to Mack Wilson Sr. in the front seven.
The Cardinals appear intent on using both Cody Simon and Jack Gibbens based on what packages offensive personnel are showing. Gibbens is more slated for pass coverage while Simon could be their guy on early run downs.
It should be an interesting mix of rotations until one of the two can really separate themselves as a legitimate starter — or the Cardinals truly do deploy a rotating door at the position.
Defensive coordinator Nick Rallis spent the last three seasons with prior head coach Jonathan Gannon heavily involved in defensive scheming/game-planning, though Gannon says Rallis was the play-caller.
Gannon was fired earlier this offseason, and the Cardinals couldn't find another suitable replacement for their DC — ultimately retaining Rallis for a fourth season. With LaFleur's expertise strictly coming on the offensive side of the ball, Rallis has free rein.
But something needs to change. Something needs to be different.
Rallis' leash is extremely short entering the regular season. The Cardinals had one of the league's worst units on the defensive side of the ball, and while injuries played a major factor there — Rallis can't run back the same thinking and operation he did last season.
This question, though listed last, could perhaps be the biggest in determining the Cardinals' success this season.

title: Jacoby Brissett’s Cardinals Teammates Just Sent a Clear Message
full_text:
ARIZONA — To the outside world, Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett is a mere bridge quarterback to hold the fort down until a long-term answer is there.
Plenty of QB rankings have Brissett near the bottom of the league while a healthy majority of Cardinals fans were displeased over Brissett's 1-11 record as a starter, or his contract holdout that bled into training camp, or both.
However, within the walls of the team's facility in Tempe, a fairly loud message was sent on Brissett.
Brissett was voted one of five Cardinals team captains ahead of the 2026 season, joining the likes of Hjalte Froholdt, Casey Kreiter, Budda Baker and Mack Wilson Sr. in the process. Head coach Mike LaFleur says only players in the locker room voted.
It's not often where a journeyman passer gets that coveted "C" on his chest, though Brissett obviously has earned the respect of his peers.
"That wasn't shocking to me, just in terms of his interaction with not just the offense, but this whole team," LaFleur said on Brissett getting the nod as a team captain.
"The more and more I'm around him, the more I get it in terms of the person. Always knew it from afar, but just having that first however long it's been seven weeks or so of being with him, it's been great."
From the public perspective, it may have been a bit shocking. For those who are consistently around the team every week, previous players have made their feelings quite clear on Brissett — even when he was still in the midst of a contract dispute with the organization.
"It was exciting to see him here," star tight end Trey McBride said on having Brissett present at mandatory minicamp.
"Guys want him to be here. We would love to have him in the building but he's working through some things on his own and we totally understand that. You could just tell the presence he brought today, it was awesome."
Star safety Budda Baker also offered:
"No matter what any player says, he just wants the team to be good and ultimately win games. I think Jacoby did a great job last year. I know we didn't get the wins we wanted, but I think he held command of the offense at a high level.”
Are the Cardinals planning on having Brissett around long-term? Not close — though the respect he has from the very men he'll be entering a weekly battle with is so glaringly obvious.

title: Jacoby Brissett Headlines List of 2026 Arizona Cardinals Team Captains
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals announced their 2026 team captains today.
According to head coach Mike LaFleur, QB Jacoby Brissett, OL Hjalte Froholdt, LS Casey Kreiter, DB Budda Baker and LB Mack Wilson will be captains this season. LaFleur says the vote was held strictly by players in the locker room.
"Whether you're a captain or not a captain, you be who you are within your own personality. However, when you do get voted a captain, obviously that's kind of saying that your teammates, the locker room, looks up to you," LaFleur said.
"I can't think of five better people to look up to in terms of just guys that are going to keep it real with each other, hold people to standards, communicate with me. I don't need to know everything that's going on in locker room, I just need to know the stuff that's pertinent.
"Just because it's just those five doesn't mean that there aren't other guys. I mean, there was quite a few guys that I won't mention that were right up there in the running for it, and those guys are still going to have a voice too. Some of it's going to be through the silent tape, if that makes sense, because that's about as important as anything. Not what you say, but actually what you're doing."
LaFleur also gave an update on Cardinals running back Jeremiyah Love — you can find out more about that here .
Kreiter is the lone newcomer to Arizona this offseason to land as a captain while the offense and defense both have two representatives on their respective sides of the ball. All of Baker, Wilson and Froholdt are returning captains from last season.
Brissett steps into the role of both captain and full-time starter in Arizona this season. Despite outside noise and narratives after a lengthy contract battle that was eventually settled early into training camp, the Cardinals have been ultra high on Brissett — both on and off the field.
"That wasn't shocking to me, just in terms of his interaction with not just the offense, but this whole team," LaFleur said of Brissett being voted a captain.
"The more and more I'm around him, the more I get it in terms of the person. Always knew it from afar, but just having that first however long it's been seven weeks or so of being with him, it's been great."
Brissett is all but settled into his seat as Arizona's QB1 to begin the regular season, which begins Sunday when the Cardinals travel to face the Los Angeles Chargers.

title: Cardinals' Jeremiyah Love Gets Promising Injury Update Before Week 1
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are officially in a game week, and all eyes are on running back Jeremiyah Love.
The third overall pick suffered a reported high ankle sprain during preseason action against the Las Vegas Raiders and hasn't practiced or played in a preseason game since.
Now, as the Cardinals gear up for their season opener against the Los Angeles Chargers, head coach Mike LaFleur appears to be optimistic regarding Love's chances of playing this week.
"Progressing. He was out there moving around today. So we'll see on Wednesday, I'll have a better idea for all those guys that I know you guys are going to ask about on Wednesday," LaFleur told reporters.
When specifically asked if he was optimistic on Love playing, LaFleur said, "Yeah, I feel good."
Love was injured on his final of 14 touches against the Raiders, which included a few highlight plays before exiting action. The Cardinals were fairly positive on Love's injury being minor, though the next few days produced some larger concerns. Love missed the last two preseason games and has been sidelined since.
Love's ability as both a runner and receiver can elevate the Cardinals' offense to new levels, and the small taste we got of Arizona's new weapon in Vegas was extremely exciting.
Love displayed everything that made him great as a Heisman finalist at Notre Dame: Instincts, balance, speed and power all seemingly carried over to the NFL level — at least through camp practice and the one half of preseason action.
When fully healthy, Love can be a vital part of the team's offense for 2026 and beyond.
We'll get our first injury report for this week on Wednesday, where it's very likely Love will be labeled either as a non-participant or limited due to his ankle injury.
With the Cardinals playing things safe on the conservative side of injuries — it wouldn't be a surprise to see Love made a game-time decision in Los Angeles.

title: 4 Roster Decisions That Will Define the Cardinals Season
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals ' regular season is here.
After months of roster moves, workouts, speculation and training camp/preseason action, the Cardinals enter the first week of the Mike LaFLeur era with hopes of potentially shocking the NFL world.
These four roster decisions will play a big part in shaping the team's 2026 season :
How it will impact Cardinals: Beck isn't the Week 1 starter, and after making just one appearance in preseason due to injuries, who knows when Arizona may see their rookie quarterback in action again? The kicker here is Beck's status will largely dictate what the Cardinals could do in next year's quarterback market.
That makes playing Beck nearly imperative for the organization at some point this regular season. Jacoby Brissett's leash, with Beck looming behind, is just a tad shorter as a result. With that established, Arizona's quarterback room is far from settled — and Beck very well could force the Cardinals into a quarterback change at some point this season.
How it will impact Cardinals: Arizona's offense welcomed the draft's top playmaker to their backfield, upping the ceiling for the unit and adding a dynamic presence that truly could push the Cardinals near the top of the league in terms of potential.
Love is capable of doing damage through both the passing and rushing attack. He's not your typical running back — he's capable of doing practically anything asked out of a skill position player. If he lives up to the hype, the Cardinals' offense improves almost overnight, and perhaps Arizona's able to keep up in some track meets they previously couldn't as a result.
How it will impact Cardinals: It's impossible to ask the Cardinals (or any team) to replinish every hole across the roster. Front offices consistently battle what areas to improve and what positions to leave short. This offseason, Arizona revamped their rushing attack and left their edge room untouched.
The Cardinals again will rely on a pass rush that ranked in the bottom five of team sacks and pressures last season. Josh Sweat is great, though the rest of his position leaves a ton left to be desired. Arizona again is shaping up to be questionable on the defensive side of the ball, mostly thanks to their glaring need for another strong pass rusher.
How it will impact Cardinals: The Cardinals attempted to upgrade their right guard spot with second-round pick Chase Bisontis, though the organization is taking a massive bet on Elijah Wilkinson as their starting right tackle.
The offensive line is only as strong as its weakest link. Wilkinson will be tasked with stepping up his game after allowing 46 pressures and six sacks last season — which topped Atlanta's offensive line. He also had 12 penalties.
That's not going to fly in Arizona, and the Cardinals' right side of the offensive line might struggle early and often if Wilkinson isn't able to maximize a fresh start.
